summary: First-derivative edge detectors such as Sobel, Prewitt, Roberts and Scharr measure absolute grey-level differences. We revisit the log-gradient magnitude, a relative-gradient edge operator, and motivate it by analogy with the superderivative, a multiplicative derivative in which the independent variable is perturbed multiplicatively rather than additively. In one and two dimensions the logarithm of the superderivative is a radial logarithmic derivative; its local, origin-free, isotropic analogue is the magnitude of the logarithmic gradient. The resulting operator measures relative rather than absolute change, giving an edge-strength map that is invariant under global intensity rescaling. We present the theory, show how the operator can be implemented in two steps---a classical gradient kernel plus a pointwise division---and compare it with standard first-derivative filters on synthetic images with ground-truth edges and on the official BSDS500 benchmark. We also study a parametric family that interpolates between the absolute gradient and the log-gradient; empirically, the best members are small intermediate exponents, which edge the classical kernels by a small but statistically detectable margin in the per-image metric and, with the same Gaussian smoothing as the single-$σ$ Canny, match it in ODS and lead it in OIS and AP, while the tuned Canny remains ahead in ODS. The single-threshold margin over the kernels does not replicate on the held-out test split, and the fully relative endpoint is never the best member, its ranking depending on the edge-map normalisation. The contribution is the construction and the invariance it buys, not a new state of the art.

title: An Analysis of High-Dimensional Land-Water Transitions in the Great Lakes via a Bayesian Discrepancy Model for Multinomial Data
summary: Global water-level systems have undergone large changes in recent years. Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) land cover data can be used to monitor and understand these changes. However, such data are extremely high-dimensional making them difficult to process while accounting for all sources of uncertainty. Bayesian hierarchical models are commonly implemented using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods which can be computationally expensive for large datasets. Exact Posterior Regression (EPR) provides an efficient alternative for inference in latent Gaussian hierarchical models under exponential families without requiring MCMC or approximate Bayesian strategies. EPR has not been developed for multinomial data, and we extend this class of models to the multinomial setting. Additionally, we explore signal-to-noise covariance properties of discrepancy models, which we expect to be present in our data. We extend EPR to multinomial likelihoods via a stick-breaking construction to analyze water-level changes. Through simulation studies, we compare the proposed multinomial EPR approach with alternative models implemented using Gibbs sampling and the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). We evaluate each approach based on regression parameter estimation, category probability estimation, and computational efficiency. Overall, EPR and INLA achieve substantial reductions in computation time while EPR shows improved metrics in estimation and prediction.

title: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery
summary: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.

title: MiDiff: MIDI-Conditioned Diffusion Models for Drum Audio Enhancement
comment: 13 pages. Submitted to IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing. Audio demos and code: https://midiff-paper.github.io/midiff-project-page/
summary: Bridging the semantic gap between perfect symbolic musical structure and severely degraded acoustic signals offers a powerful paradigm for high-fidelity audio restoration. We introduce MiDiff, a diffusion-based generative model for drum audio enhancement that conditions the reverse process on temporally aligned Musical Instrument Digital Interface (MIDI) piano rolls. We extend the Score-Based Generative Models for Speech Enhancement (SGMSE) framework in the complex Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) domain by integrating a pretrained MIDI encoder, multi-scale temporal alignment, and three complementary conditioning strategies: early injection, Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), and cross-attention. We further show that providing the same piano roll only through classifier guidance, driven by an Automatic Drum Transcription (ADT) model on the audio-only score, yields no measurable gain: the symbolic prior is effective when it conditions the score network. To relax the requirement for ground-truth MIDI at inference, we further propose a hybrid reverse schedule that transcribes the diffusion state online with the same noise-aware ADT network and hands over from the audio-only score to MiDiff at a tunable switch time, cutting test FAD by 47% relative to the audio-only baseline without any symbolic input (switch time selected on the test set). We train our model on the StemGMD dataset using a non-additive degradation pipeline that simulates room reverberation with echo, electret capsule frequency response, and soft-clipping saturation with noise. MiDiff substantially outperforms the SGMSE baseline in terms of Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) on both the validation and held-out test sets. Ablation studies demonstrate that combining all three conditioning strategies yields superior performance and that authentic MIDI velocity dynamics are critical for effective symbolic conditioning.

title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
summary: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.

title: Threshold Compatibility and Support-Selection Diagnostics in Neural Discovery of Partial Differential Equations
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Accurate regression need not yield the correct equation after support selection. For a median/sample-standard-deviation threshold in neural PDE discovery, we derive an exact two-signal retention boundary and a complete-vector perturbation bound. Exact advection-diffusion libraries lose diffusion despite coefficient recovery to numerical precision. True-support refits of forty saved sparse states reduce diffusion error without restoring all derivative accuracy. A fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator recovers exact support in sixty ideal controls but selects extra terms in every learned state. All-fold correct-support candidates are rejected by conditional validation; post hoc energy pooling preserves their higher minimum loss in all sixty states. Supplied-support estimates outperform unchanged selected equations in all 240 physical-residual comparisons on four unused analytic trajectories. With coefficients, observation points and weights fixed, exact replacement of the learned library and target reverses their learned-row ordering in 59/60 states. Weighting both losses also fails the specified Burgers diffusion-benefit criterion at every tested budget. These finite diagnostics distinguish threshold incompatibility, refit damage and score rejection; they establish neither automatic correction nor general recovery or predictive stability.

title: SelectSep: Target-Selective Video Queries for Audio Source Separation
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: Video-queried sound separation (VQSS) aims to isolate a target sound from an audio mixture using its corresponding video as a query. However, scene-level video queries can become ambiguous when multiple sounding objects are visible, particularly when the target and interferer are semantically similar. We propose SelectSep, a target-selective VQSS framework that jointly uses text and a single click coordinate to specify the target source and instance without requiring segmentation at inference time. We adapt the visual encoder through target-feature distillation with text and click conditioning, and then fine-tune the separator using the adapted visual features. We also introduce an on-screen interference setting, where both the target and interferer are visible, to evaluate target selectivity. Experiments on standard benchmarks and the on-screen interference setting demonstrate consistent improvements in separation quality and target selectivity, particularly for mixtures containing semantically similar sources.

title: Convex Mixed-Integer Programming for Invariant Predictions from Multi-environment Data
summary: Heterogeneous data provide an opportunity to identify causal predictors by revealing which predictive relationships remain invariant. Under a linear model, we introduce a least-squares coefficient-and-risk (LSCR) invariance principle, requiring both ordinary least squares coefficients and prediction risks to remain constant across environments. Our model neither specifies an intervention mechanism nor assumes a structural causal model for the entire system. We develop an invariance score that quantifies departures from LSCR invariance and use its optimization to construct two complementary procedures for causal predictor identification. First, we propose an estimator that jointly minimizes prediction risk and invariance penalty, and establish non-asymptotic guarantees for estimation and recovery of the causal parents under suitable identifiability conditions. Second, without requiring full identifiability, we develop a testing procedure that minimizes the invariance score over all predictor sets excluding a given variable, enabling valid causal discoveries with asymptotic error control via a multiplier bootstrap. Both procedures admit convex mixed-integer optimization formulations that avoid exhaustive subset enumeration while providing certificates of optimality. Simulations and real data experiments demonstrate substantial statistical and computational improvements over existing methods.

title: Predicate Neuron: Differentiable Quantization of Predicate Relations in Gradient-based Learning
summary: In machine learning, symbolic reasoning approaches often rely on static architectures that hinder integration into deep neural networks and gradient-based optimization. To address this, we introduce the Native Predicate Neuron, a differentiable logic-reasoning neural module that enriches standard architectures with symbolic reasoning capabilities via first-order logic quantization. The proposed neuron models relational logic by learning to alternate between operations using a single trainable parameter. It features a tailored gradient mechanism with a dual-nature formulation: executing hard logical operations during training while maintaining differentiability for backpropagation. By quantizing both its input and choice state, the Predicate Neuron approximates continuous and non-continuous functions, effectively resolving discontinuities that standard deep learning architectures struggle with. We evaluate the Predicate Neuron across Fully-Connected, Convolutional, Recurrent, and Transformer architectures on benchmarks like MNIST and Wikitext. Results show that incorporating Predicate Neurons accelerates convergence, boosts accuracy, and lowers loss in general, with particularly strong improvements in tasks requiring monotonic reasoning or handling discontinuities. Overall, the Predicate Neuron natively integrates into standard neural networks to enable fuzzy logic operations and is available in Keras and PyTorch.

title: Finite-State Uncertainty-Aware Widely-Linear Equalization for Aeronautical GMSK Links
summary: Aeronautical and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) receivers must equalize doubly selective channels under synchronization uncertainty and limited onboard computation and memory. We propose a finite-state, uncertainty-aware widely-linear (WL) equalization algorithm for Gaussian minimum-shift keying (GMSK) links. The algorithm uses synchronization estimates and their reliability descriptors to select one of a small number of precomputed filters, avoiding repeated online coefficient synthesis. Using a finite-memory Laurent model, we design the stored affine WL filters from conditional physical-state moments. We derive an exact characterization of excess mean-square error (MSE) relative to adaptation to continuous side information, Lloyd-type conditions for finite-state design, local timing--frequency mismatch certificates, and an orthogonal decomposition of design and information losses. On a reference channel at $E_b/N_0=8$~dB under high synchronization-estimation uncertainty, a $16$-state bank reduces pseudo-symbol MSE by $51.9\%$ relative to point-estimate WL time-varying MMSE equalization and by $6.6\%$ relative to posterior-mean (PM) substitution. With identical partitioning, routing, and storage, conditional-moment filters reduce MSE by $10.1\%$ and full-waveform average bit error rate (ABER) by $15.6\%$ relative to representative-state filters. Across $18$ synthetic three-path channels with individually fitted banks, MSE and ABER decrease by $5.3\%$ and $12.9\%$, respectively, relative to PM substitution. The $16$-state receiver stores $2048$ real coefficients. Posterior integration, robustness sweeps, and software timing measurements quantify the tradeoff between equalization accuracy, online computational cost, and bank refresh.

title: Noise Calibration and Exact Recovery for Multiview Ordinal Rearrangement Data
summary: We studied simultaneous recovery of a latent group count, subject partition, and signature means from multiview ordinal ranks. A normalized reference rearrangement score is an affine Spearman correlation; the problem concerns the information retained by several such scores and their noise geometry. We develop an ordered-gap estimator with direction-specific concentration radii. Its finite-sample guarantee separates signature noise, missing groups, and candidate coverage, and allows the group count to grow under an attainable-margin condition. A coordinatewise partition followed by label-tuple refinement recovers groups even when every individual coordinate has population collisions. A binary-code construction explains why the one-dimensional inverse-group margin restriction need not govern a retained coordinate bank. We derive actual-law concentration from bounded ranking modules and a fixed-dimensional combinatorial central limit theorem under an observed permutation representation. A binary ordinal submodel gives logarithmic exact-recovery information scales. A subject-effect construction distinguishes persistent overlap from reducible measurement noise, and an additional ordinal anchor quantifies how new information lowers that error floor. Five focused simulation scenarios illustrate direction-specific calibration, growing-group recovery, coordinate collision resolution, variance reduction, and the effect of an additional ordinal anchor.

title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.

title: Wav2Aug: A Drop-In Speech Augmentation Policy
summary: SpecAugment is the dominant speech augmentation policy, but researchers have studied it primarily for automatic speech recognition (ASR), and it operates on spectrograms, limiting its applicability to other speech tasks and waveform models. We propose Wav2Aug, a drop-in waveform augmentation policy that randomly samples two augmentations from a calibrated pool of waveform transformations. We calibrate the augmentation hyperparameters once and reuse them across tasks and architectures, eliminating task-specific tuning. Experiments on ten speech benchmarks show that Wav2Aug achieves ASR performance comparable to SpecAugment while improving over it on average across non-ASR tasks, yielding an average relative error reduction of 12.8% over the strongest compatible SpecAugment baseline. We further show that multi-view training provides additional gains, with two augmented views offering the best tradeoff between performance and computational cost.

title: A Spectral Boundary for Independence Learnability
summary: Learning independence is fundamental to statistical inference and machine learning, yet learning independence between entire time series by a test remains challenging when only a single observation record is available. Existing guarantees often rely on structural or mixing assumptions, while stationarity and ergodicity alone do not permit consistent testing. In this work, we identify a class-level boundary governed by shared nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues, which represent common persistent oscillatory frequencies of the two processes. When no such eigenvalues are shared, we extend shift-based rank calibration with finite-window dependence witnesses and a data-adaptive threshold to construct a deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control, without quantitative mixing assumptions. Conversely, we show that no possibly randomized test can achieve vanishing false-positive probabilities under every independent jointly totally ergodic law while consistently detecting every dependent jointly totally ergodic law with a shared nontrivial eigenvalue. This impossibility already holds for binary observations and persists within any prescribed nonempty open eigenvalue window, identifying a spectral obstruction to universal learning of full-process independence.

title: Pooled Testing under Congestion: Operational Scaling Laws for Pool-Size Selection
summary:
Classical pooled-testing rules choose pool sizes to reduce the number of tests. In practice, however, samples arrive over time, pools take time to form, testing capacity is finite, and positive pools create bursts of follow-up work. These operational features can make the test-efficient pool size far from the delay-efficient one.
  We formulate pooled testing with stochastic arrivals and finite testing capacity as a queueing system, and derive exact performance representations and asymptotic scaling laws for fixed-batch Dorfman testing and a dynamic two-threshold policy. The analysis reveals three distinct design regimes. When test usage is the main concern, the classical Dorfman rule is recovered and the optimal pool size scales with the inverse square root of prevalence. When delay accumulated while the laboratory is busy testing another batch matters, positive pools create service-time variability that grows more rapidly with pool size than the mean retesting burden, and the optimal scale shifts to the inverse cube root of prevalence. When waiting to assemble a pool is itself costly, the optimal fixed pool size remains bounded even as prevalence becomes very small. Under severe capacity scarcity, congestion remains relevant at the classical Dorfman scale: the square-root law survives, but with a capacity-dependent constant.
  Dynamic pooling separates two operational decisions that fixed pool sizes conflate. A lower threshold determines when routine testing should begin, while an upper threshold limits pooling when backlog is high. The lower threshold follows the cube-root scale, whereas the upper threshold primarily acts as congestion control. The results show how prevalence, capacity, and delay jointly determine pooling decisions and explain why operationally optimal pools can be much smaller than those suggested by test-efficiency calculations alone.

title: Minimum-Time Trajectory for Escort-Assisted Evasion from a Sensing-Limited Pursuer
summary: This paper studies a minimum-time path-planning problem in which an escort assists a leader by triggering and redirecting a sensing-limited pursuer. For the post-engagement case with equal leader, escort, and pursuer speeds, we show that the minimum-time leader trajectory has a three-phase structure: an initial straight segment, a moving-boundary segment, and a final straight segment to the goal. The boundary-following kinematics and the corresponding entry and exit conditions are derived and used to construct the leader trajectory for a fixed escort engagement direction. The engagement direction is then optimized over the feasible set to obtain the minimum-time solution. Numerical results illustrate the resulting trajectory and the benefits of escort assistance.

title: Modular Bayesian Foundation Models: Bayesian time series encoders for OOD detection, routing and forecasting
summary: Industrial systems continuously generate time series that vary in sampling frequency, scale, dynamics, and operating regime. Consequently a single time-series foundation model may not be able to represent all regimes effectively and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is computationally expensive. Modular foundation models address this issue by reusing specialised encoders trained on diverse datasets and by allowing the expansion of capabilities through the addition of new experts. This approach requires compact experts to minimize storage cost and a proper selection mechanism of experts for unseen data. We propose a modular foundation model framework that combines end-to-end Bayesian encoder training with uncertainty based routing. Using Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (SBNNs), we build a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection. At the selected ranks, our Bayesian collection uses 63.8\% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. We evaluate this framework on time-series data through distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing in terms of forecast MSE, while reducing average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836. It also increases PICP90 from 82.28\% to 89.03\%. In a separate model-family comparison, we evaluate the SBNN pipeline against full-rank Bayes by Backprop, deep ensembles, and MC Dropout. The SBNN pipeline achieves an average MSE of 0.390, comparable with 0.396 for deep ensembles, 0.389 for MC dropout, and 0.443 for the full-rank Bayesian model. It uses 63.9\% fewer parameters than MC dropout, 81.9\% fewer than the full-rank model, and 92.8\% fewer than the deep ensemble.

title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
summary: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$ε$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

title: Personalising Parametric Audio Effect Recommendation for Vocals from Parameter-only Style Priors
summary: Audio effect recommendation has mostly modelled style through reference audio and audio-domain losses. Because the parameter-to-audio map of parametric effects is many-to-one, such systems can match a reference without reflecting how a given engineer works. We instead model an engineer's style as a distribution over effect-chain parameters, which matches the data engineers can realistically share: console recalls store parameters without the audio they were applied to. Under a label-shift assumption, a personalised recommendation follows in closed form from a generic content model, a parameter population model and an engineer prior, with no paired engineer audio and no tuned weights. For vocal chains, the content signal is small but real, and concentrated in high-frequency EQ, dynamics and reverb. A forced-choice test with $14$ listeners found that the style-prior and content-only recommendations were distinguishable (89.3%), with results consistent with prior width affecting the balance between style and content, while parameter-space cosine does not predict perceived difference.

title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk
comment: 37 pages, 7 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information (55 pages) as an ancillary file. Pre-registered on OSF Registries (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/8HMTZ). Code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23737378; benchmark data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23737416
summary: Tabular foundation models are pretrained networks that predict risk from a table without fitting a model. Whether their risks are correct (calibrated) has been judged on real data, where true risk is unknown. In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, we compared TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2 and Mitra-v2 with Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, then on four clinical data sets. Foundation models were not a shortcut to calibration. Their calibration slope matched FLIC's within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even 3,000 patients were often not enough: with FLIC, TabPFN-3.5 or Mitra-v2, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept and slope at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%. TabICLv2 did worse (8%-39% and 1%-3%). Across the random designs, foundation models had a lower true calibration error than FLIC beyond the margin in 25%-38% and a higher one in none, though small losses were predicted at n = 3000. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations; recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.

title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
summary: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.

title: Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 11 tables, 1 algorithm. Code: https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr ; weights: https://huggingface.co/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr-kroko-en
summary: We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr.

title: Adaptive stopping and forecasting of screening, rescreening and randomization in multicentre clinical trials
summary: In randomised clinical trials, patients typically undergo some screening stages before randomisation. These stages complicate design as patients may be randomised after admissions to screening have been halted. Stopping the admission of new patients too late may lead to over-enrolment, as more patients than planned are randomised, increasing costs, unnecessary patient exposure and the time required to complete recruitment. Stopping too early may result in failure to achieve the planned sample size. Predictions of the stopping time should therefore account for patients currently in screening and the number of the patients to be randomised. We present a novel statistical framework for joint modelling screening and randomisation and determining an adaptive stopping time to stop admitting new patients to screening before the planned randomisation target is reached. The aim is to reduce over-enrolment while maintaining a high probability of achieving the target. We represent the screening and randomisation pathway as a multistage process with stage-specific durations and transition probabilities estimated from trial data. The model yields the distribution of the number of patients who will be randomised from the current screening pipeline and the probability of reaching the planned randomisation target. If this probability exceeds a specified threshold, such as 95% or 99%, admission of new patients to screening should be stopped. Otherwise, the model is updated as additional data accrue and is used to forecast future pipeline and the stopping time. The framework can incorporate scheduled site initiations and future closures using evolving stochastic processes, and supporting forecasts at global, regional and country levels. Illustrative simulations show that the approach can reduce over-enrolment substantially while preserving a high probability of reaching the target sample size.

title: Selective Transfer Learning for Groundwater Level Anomaly Forecasting: Accuracy-Risk Trade-offs
summary: This work studies context-aware selective transfer learning for multi-well groundwater anomaly forecasting in the Netherlands. Source-domain pretraining can raise average accuracy but is not uniformly reliable: it degrades performance on a substantial fraction of heterogeneous wells. Context-Aware Selective Learning (CASL) uses calibration-trained, constrained contextual blending of frozen no-transfer and fixed-transfer parents. Global Convex Blend uses the same parents with one calibration-fitted weight per seed. The corrected task requires nine consecutive observed monthly inputs and an exact three-calendar-month target, without interpolation. Evaluation covers 457 wells and 13,718 test windows under five predefined seeds, with the four-cell maxsim0.60 source pool frozen using Always-TL validation RMSE alone. Fixed transfer harms 18.38-51.86% of wells. CASL has 0.424-1.084% lower RMSE than No TL, partially rescuing 97.53-99.50% and fully rescuing 23.46-43.78% of fixed-harmed wells. Partial rescue can arise structurally from convex blending and does not establish contextual superiority. Global Convex Blend protects more wells in four seeds, while CASL has slightly lower pooled RMSE in four. Neither dominates: the results support an accuracy-risk trade-off on the fixed split, not rolling deployment validity.

title: Channel State Information-Free Angle Spoofing for Differential Localization Privacy
summary: This paper proposes a channel state information (CSI)-free angle spoofing strategy that remains effective even when the eavesdropper (Eve) uses differential statistics to estimate the location of the transmitter (Alice). Specifically, by designing a precoding matrix, Eve incorrectly estimates the angle differences of departure (ADoDs), thereby spoofing Alice's location. Meanwhile, the trusted user (Bob) can still infer Alice's true location with a modest amount of securely shared side information. Given the channel parameters estimated by Eve from the spoofed channel, the resulting localization bias introduced to the eavesdroppers under the spoofed geometric is analyzed. Eve's bias can be driven to infinity asymptotically in a key parameter of the precoder. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method introduces significant localization errors for Eve. When combined with a prior CSI-free spoofing strategy, further degraded performance is achieved by Eve.

title: Joint optimisation of interim timing and stopping boundaries in group sequential trials
summary: Group sequential designs (GSDs) are common in confirmatory trials, and their efficiency depends jointly on the timing of interim analyses and the shape of stopping boundaries. Most existing approaches optimise one component while holding the other fixed. Joint optimisation over free critical values has been studied for two- and three-stage efficacy-only designs and for tests with binding futility boundaries. Here we jointly optimise the full interim schedule and the boundary shape within the Hwang-Shih-DeCani and Kim-DeMets spending families, minimising the expected sample size under a specified alternative while controlling overall type I and type II error rates. A convex error-spending constraint prevents excessive early type I error spending. On the canonical information scale, the joint optimum depends only on the error rates, number of analyses and spending family, and is invariant to endpoint type and effect size. Without the convexity constraint, the parametric optima reproduced the unrestricted optima of Brittain & Bailey (1993) to within 0.001 in expected inflation factor. For three or more looks the jointly optimal design Pareto-dominated the scheduling-only optimal Pocock design, achieving the same or smaller expected sample size with uniformly smaller maximum sample size. Under a prespecified 1% tolerance, six analyses, five interim plus a final, captured essentially all efficiency attainable with up to seven analyses, reducing expected sample size by 23% and 33% at 80% and 90% power relative to the fixed-sample design. We illustrate the approach by redesigning the CORRECT trial.

title: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills
summary: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a SKILL.md file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.

title: Structured Pruning of Feedback Delay Networks
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the IEEE Open Journal of Signal Processing
summary: Feedback delay networks (FDNs) are recursive filter structures used to synthesise artificial reverberation. Their feedback matrix governs both energy exchange between delay lines and the computation required at every sample, making its design central to balancing an FDN's acoustic performance and implementation efficiency. In this work, we develop an FDN-specific structured pruning method that connects these acoustic and computational concerns, allowing high-order dense orthogonal designs to be fitted to efficient implementations. The feedback matrix is replaced by stages of fixed permutations and small orthogonal blocks. We characterise connectivity growth with the network depth and derive exact conditional block updates for matrix fitting, followed by refinement against the reference FDN magnitude response. The resulting factors admit direct vectorised evaluation, with arithmetic cost and coefficient storage scaling linearly with network size for fixed block size and depth. On an Apple M2, the selected staged kernels achieve feedback-multiplication speedups over dense BLAS ranging from approximately threefold to over twentyfold across the tested network sizes, while substantially reducing coefficient storage. Objective metrics and listening tests indicate that the proposed staged approximations closely preserve the spectral and temporal character of their dense references. An analysis of processor utilisation and register reuse explains why execution time depends on more than the operation count. Finally, block size and depth provide practical control over response fidelity, storage, and real-time cost, allowing acoustic design to precede the choice of an efficient implementation.

title: Adaptive Bayesian Estimation of Conditional Densities Based on Orthogonal Polynomials
summary: We study Bayesian estimation of conditional densities represented by normalized squares of orthogonal polynomial series. We specify the conditional density without modeling the marginal distribution of covariates. A prior on smoothness, the number of terms, and the coefficients gives adaptive posterior contraction at the minimax rate without a logarithmic factor when the normalized square-root representation of the true density is bounded away from zero and sufficiently smooth. For one outcome and $d_x$ covariates, the rate over classes with degree smoothness $s$ is $n^{-s/(2s+d_x+1)}$. The posterior predictive density attains the corresponding minimax squared Hellinger risk. For bounded nonnegative representations in Legendre and Chebyshev classes, we establish the minimax rate at every $s>0$. A prior that also permits a small mixture with the reference density adapts over these classes up to a logarithmic factor and retains the exact rate on the positive, sufficiently smooth subclass. Additional results concern identification, conditional distribution functions and quantiles, coefficient recovery and uniform convergence, independent Gaussian coefficient priors, and selection of polynomial terms.

title: Anisotropic Trust Region Warping for Prior-Data Fitted Networks in Bayesian Optimisation
comment: Accepted at the 2026 NeurIPS Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning (OPT). 18 pages, 12 figures
summary: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) replace the hyperparameter refitting of Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates in Bayesian optimisation with a single forward pass, at the cost of a prior that is fixed at meta-training time. We show empirically that a PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls increasingly behind that of a refitted GP as the objective function's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the PFN's meta-training prior, and that this deficit carries over to optimisation performance. To correct the mismatch without retraining the network, we introduce Anisotropic Trust Region (ATR) warping. Per-dimension lengthscales are estimated by kernel target alignment, and an affine rescaling of the input space maps the objective onto the lengthscale the PFN expects, with a trust region around the anchor determining which observations are retained, leaving the PFN's $\mathcal{O}(d \cdot N^2)$ inference cost unchanged. On functions drawn from a Matérn-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves optimisation performance of the PFN at both extremes of the lengthscale range. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/Trust-Region-Warping-For-PFNs.

title: A Sub-Aperture-Based Ray-Tracing Framework for Near-Field U-MIMO THz Communications
summary: Terahertz (THz) communications are characterized by antennas with large apertures and extended near-field (NF) region, offering the opportunity to develop adaptable beam manipulation strategies, particularly related to ultra-massive MIMO (U-MIMO). While Ray-Tracing (RT) offers an attractive alternative to full-wave methods, conventional ray-based approaches are generally formulated under far-field (FF) assumptions. We propose a technique that extends RT to the NF regime, enabling ray-based NF characterization of transmitting arrays. We model the transmitting array as an antenna aperture and develop a RT framework that partitions the transmitting aperture into sub-apertures emitting FF contributions which can be propagated via geometric optics (GO). We develop a Ray-Launching algorithm based on the proposed framework and assess its beam-reconstruction accuracy against full-wave propagation. The results demonstrate that, through tunable aperture partitioning, the proposed approach can reproduce beam manipulation effects characteristic of NF U-MIMO THz communications using GO ray propagation.

title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
comment: Submitted to a peer-reviewed journal; 16 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables
summary: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). Under such rank-deficient rarity ($n_1 < p$), maximum likelihood estimators suffer from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood methods exhibit severe intercept bias, and convex minority oversampling techniques such as SMOTE collapse into an $(n_1 - 1)$-dimensional affine subspace. In this paper, we propose a novel \textit{Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement} estimator that shifts the paradigm from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Grounded in Stein's Lemma, we prove that the conditional expectation shift of the abundant majority class ($Y=0$) induced by logistic truncation uniquely identifies the true hyperplane normal $\boldsymbolβ$ after Mahalanobis whitening. We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). To accommodate both semi-supervised environments (with an unlabeled background mean) and strictly supervised subsamples, we introduce a hybrid estimator incorporating the intrinsic third-moment skewness of the majority class alongside a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and real-world benchmark applications (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) under extreme rarity ($n_1 \in \{3, 5\}$) demonstrate that our approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth's regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.

title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files
summary: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.

title: From Local to Global: Sheaf-Theoretic Control Barrier Functions on Manifolds
summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide formal safety guarantees for dynamical systems by rendering a safe set forward-invariant via pointwise-optimal feedback control. While the CBF framework is well established for dynamical systems in Euclidean space, there exist gaps for systems evolving on non-Euclidean manifolds. For systems modeled as constrained control differential inclusions, we introduce the Sheaf-CBF: a sheaf-theoretic framework for CBFs on smooth manifolds and vector bundles. The differential inclusions are formulated intrinsically on the control bundle, and analogous regularity properties in the Euclidean case are established fiberwise under local trivializations. Regularity conditions are given under which a pointwise-optimal feedback law is single-valued and continuous over local charts. Framed as a local-to-global optimization problem, sheaf-theoretic restriction and gluing compatibility conditions on overlapping charts are shown to uniquely determine a continuous global section of the control bundle, thereby guaranteeing forward invariance of the safe set. Numerical simulations on a nontrivial M{ö}bius strip demonstrate that failure of sheaf compatibility results in violations of safety, whereas the Sheaf-CBF maintains forward invariance.

title: On the median of the beta distribution in relation to the median of the gamma distribution
comment: 49 pages, 11 figures. The Lean 4 formalization and Python code that reproduces the figures and numerical checks are in the ancillary files
summary: The median of the beta distribution has no closed form, but it is closely tied to the median of the gamma distribution. Kerman's approximation has the ratio form $g(α)/(g(α)+g(β))$ with $g(x) = x - 1/3$, a lower bound on the gamma median, and it is a lower bound on the beta median for $1/3 < α< β$. The ratio form built from the true gamma median is a tighter lower bound, asymptotically exact as $β\to \infty$. The ratio form built from the Wilson-Hilferty approximation to the gamma median, implicit in a classical approximation to the $F$ distribution but little known as an approximation to the beta median, is an upper bound on the edge $α= 1$ and for large shape parameters. The ratio form that is exact on the lines $α= 1$ and $β= 1$ yields a new approximation to the gamma median, which is an upper bound on it for shape parameter below 1 and a lower bound above 1; no ratio form gives the beta median exactly. For large shape parameters, the logit of the median has an explicit second-order expansion. For small shape parameters, bounds in elementary functions are asymptotically tight, and odds-corrected forms of the low-$α$ asymptote, with an elementary factor that is exact on the edges $α= 1$ and $β= 1$, are, numerically, one-sided bounds within 0.44% of the median that are exact on the lines $α= 1$, $β= 1$, and $α= β$. Steering their exponents with four fitted constants, and interpolating between two ratio forms where both shape parameters exceed 1, gives an approximation in elementary functions that is exact on those lines and numerically within 0.065% of the median over the whole domain. Most of the proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4.

title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.

title: Joint Antenna Position and Beamforming Optimization for Movable Antenna Enabled Near-Field ISAC Imaging
summary: Near-field (NF) integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems enable simultaneous two-dimensional (2D) radar imaging and multi-user downlink communication. However, fixed-position antenna arrays can exhibit high sidelobes in the point spread function (PSF), which degrade imaging performance and cause ghost-target artifacts. Movable antennas (MAs) offer additional spatial degrees of freedom to suppress these sidelobes while meeting communication requirements, without increasing the number of antenna elements. In this paper, we investigate MA-enabled NF ISAC by jointly optimizing the transmit and receive antenna positions and the transmit beamforming to minimize a weighted sum of the integrated sidelobe level (ISL) and peak sidelobe level (PSL) of the 2D PSF, subject to communication-rate, illumination-power, transmit-power, and antenna-placement constraints. To tackle the resulting non-convex problem, we propose a hybrid alternating optimization (AO) framework that combines particle swarm optimization with a genetic algorithm. Our numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves the lowest ISL among the considered array configurations and reduces the PSL by at least 5 dB compared with the benchmarks. The optimized array is further shown to resolve two closely spaced targets whose reflectivities differ by 6dB, outperforming random, Mills Cross, and rectangular arrays while satisfying the imposed minimum user-throughput requirements.

title: Sparse Directed Network Recovery From Multivariate Count Time Series
summary: Count time series arise naturally in many scientific applications. Examples include species abundances collected over time, and gene expression counts over pseudotime. Network inference from such data can yield important insight into underlying biological mechanisms, but is challenging because count observations are discrete, overdispersed, and temporally dependent. We propose a multivariate Poisson log-normal model in which observed counts arise from a Poisson distribution with rates determined by a latent vector autoregressive (VAR) process. The latent VAR transition matrix induces directed temporal dependencies among components and serves as the target network parameter. We establish identifiability of the model under suitable conditions and develop two procedures for sparse estimation of the VAR transition matrix. Our first estimator is a sparse method-of-moments estimator, for which we establish consistent network recovery and parameter estimation in high-dimensional settings. Our second estimator is an L1-penalized variational inference estimator that is motivated by recent approaches for count data. We evaluate the proposed estimators through simulations under a range of sampling regimes. We further demonstrate the method on a macroinvertebrate abundance time series collected from European freshwater ecosystems, obtaining an interpretable ecological network.

title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
summary: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.

title: Computationally Constrained First-Order Prediction-Correction Approach for Time-Varying Convex Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, for submission to ECC
summary: Time-varying optimization methods often predict the locations of time-varying optima, then sample the objective function being minimized, and then compute corrections to those predictions. However, those works typically do not account for settings in which computations are limited. Therefore, in this work we formulate a prediction-correction algorithm that is designed to obey constraints on the total number of iterations it can execute over a given time horizon. We first show that there is a critical threshold for the average number of computations that can be executed between samples of the objective. Then, we show that if the number of allowable computations is above this threshold, then the distance to a time-varying optimum bound decays geometrically. Next, we show that if the number of allowable computations is below that threshold, then the distance to a time-varying optimum still remains bounded. Therefore, it is still possible to track time-varying optima with bounded error even under restrictive limits on the number of computations that can be executed. We also present an algorithm to determine how many prediction and correction steps should be executed for each sample of the objective. Simulation results show that under typical conditions our approach reduces cumulative tracking error by 45.5% compared to a comparable baseline approach.

title: TwinPoSI: Statistical Twins for Powerful Post-Selection Inference on Population-Based Regression Coefficients
summary: Post-selection inference (PoSI) quantifies uncertainty about regression coefficients after data-driven feature selection. A central question is the inferential target. Projection-based targets are the coefficients of the best linear approximation restricted to the selected features and depend on the selection procedure, whereas population-based targets are the selected features' coefficients in the full linear model and are often more relevant for scientific interpretation. The two targets can differ, even in sign. Existing PoSI methods largely focus on projection-based targets and may yield overly wide confidence intervals. We propose TwinPoSI (statistical twin post-selection inference), a method for powerful PoSI on population-based targets with false coverage rate (FCR) control. TwinPoSI leverages \textit{statistical twins}, defined as synthetic datasets generated from a fitted model to mimic the original data. With generating parameters known, statistical twins enable direct calibration of confidence intervals for bias introduced by data-dependent feature selection. We establish that TwinPoSI controls the FCR at the nominal level, up to Monte Carlo error and an asymptotically negligible approximation error. Moreover, in a Gaussian linear model with an orthogonal design, TwinPoSI uniquely attains the oracle average interval length to first order among the methods considered. Simulations show that TwinPoSI maintains reliable FCR control for both population-based and projection-based targets while yielding shorter confidence intervals and higher power than the competing methods. In riboflavin production data, TwinPoSI identifies associated genes, quantifies their directions and magnitudes of association, and yields the shortest average intervals among the methods considered.

title: Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding is used to reduce the inference cost of language models. One-step diffusion drafters propose a block of multiple tokens in parallel, reducing the sequential cost of speculative decoding. On-policy distillation trains these drafters using verifier feedback on their own proposals. However, parallel drafting makes this feedback difficult to use: the drafter predicts each token without observing the preceding tokens sampled within the same block, while the verifier conditions its prediction on those tokens. Different sampled prefixes therefore give different verifier targets for the same drafter prediction. We show that distilling against these targets separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes but unlikely after others, harming draft acceptance. We explain the effects of this mismatch and introduce Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation (MDraft), a new parallel drafter distillation method which samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes. We use all the drafts to collect information from the verifier, allowing support from alternative prefixes to influence the training target. The resulting algorithm improves the acceptance length of a parallel drafter beyond the level of pre-training, and alleviates the effects of the distributional mismatch. MDraft changes only training, retaining the drafter's architecture and inference procedure, allowing the resulting drafter to be used as-is in place of the pretrained checkpoint. Experiments on a suite of mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks show longer accepted drafts than prior distillation methods.

title: Efficient MPC for LC-Filtered Three-Level NPC Inverters in Vehicle-to-Load Applications
summary: Finite control-set model predictive control (FCS-MPC) offers fast, modulator-free voltage regulation but is sensitive to the fidelity of its internal model. This sensitivity is usually countered by algorithmic augmentation, disturbance observers, adaptive weighting, or learning-based estimators, at the cost of extra tuning and computation. This paper instead improves fidelity at the source. For a three-level neutral-point-clamped (3L-NPC) inverter with an LC output filter in vehicle-to-load operation, a coupled alpha-beta-frame predictive model carries the capacitor voltage and filter current jointly through the state vector, so that the second-order LC coupling is retained without enlarging the 27-candidate search. The cost function additionally regulates dc-link neutral-point balance and switching effort. One-step prediction accuracy, parametric sensitivity, and computational cost are bounded in closed form. Simulation of a V2L system yields a voltage total harmonic distortion of 0.72%, a steady-state tracking error of 1.6%, and transient recovery within one fundamental cycle, meeting the applicable IEEE power-quality limits with margin, without observers, parameter estimation, or learning-based augmentation.

title: Independence tests of general spatial point processes based on characteristic functions
summary: Existing nonparametric tests of spatial point process independence typically rely on random shifts to simulate their null distributions. This limits their scope to stationary point processes in rectangular study regions. Attempts to adapt random shift methods to nonrectangular study regions have resulted in significant power loss. We introduce a new type of nonparametric independence tests by taking differences of several characteristic-function-based goodness-of-fit statistics. We develop two null distribution methods for the tests without using random shifts, by making normal or symmetry assumptions on the Mercer's expansion of the test statistics. The methods are applicable to general nonstationary point processes in study regions of any shape. In simulations, our tests based on the symmetric null distribution method have better type I error control and higher power than toroidal cross-$K$ tests in most scenarios where toroidal shifts can be applied. When tested on more general settings given appropriately-fitted marginal distributions, they still have good power and almost always control the type I error well.

title: Selective and Hybrid-State Communication for Latent Multi-Agent Systems
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Resource-Aware Agentic AI (RAAAI)
summary: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware method that selectively communicates KV states while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by communicating both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks, SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7-9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one percentage point on three, and six points lower on HumanEval+. Across Qwen3.5 model scales, HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53-80% and achieves 1.16-2.78x speedups relative to text-based multi-agent communication. Together, these independently evaluated methods represent two complementary approaches to efficient latent-state communication across conventional Transformer and hybrid model architectures.

title: Semantic-Assisted Joint Channel Estimation and Symbol Detection for MU-MIMO Systems
summary: This paper presents a semantic-assisted joint channel estimation and symbol detection (Sem-JCED) receiver framework for text transmission in multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) systems. Sem-JCED integrates a linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) channel estimator, an expectation propagation (EP) symbol detector, and a semantic corrector based on ByT5, a byte-level language model. At each outer iteration, LMMSE estimates the channel from known pilots and data symbol feedback, and EP detects the data symbols. ByT5 then maps the data symbol probabilities to byte probabilities, which provide soft symbol statistics and semantic priors for feedback to LMMSE and EP, respectively, in the next iteration. Simulation results show that Sem-JCED requires about 7~dB lower signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) than conventional JCED to reach a bit error rate (BER) of $1\times10^{-2}$ with four users and four receive antennas, and outperforms maximum-likelihood detection with perfect channel knowledge over the simulated SNR range.

title: Satisficing Regret Minimization in Bandits with Knapsacks
summary: We study satisficing regret minimization in bandits with knapsacks (BwK), where a learner sequentially selects randomized policies, i.e., distributions over arms, to obtain mean rewards above a satisficing threshold as frequently as possible while respecting finite resource budgets. The performance is measured by satisficing regret, the cumulative deficits of the selected policies' mean rewards below this threshold. Resource constraints introduce two difficulties: an algorithm can incur linear satisficing regret even with small standard regret as deficits to the threshold cannot be compensated, and random consumption can cause early resource depletion even when policies are feasible in expectation. To address these challenges, we propose SELECTwK, a general algorithmic template that uses a BwK learning oracle algorithm with sub-linear expected (standard) regret upper bound to search for and test candidate satisficing policies (i.e., policies whose mean rewards exceed satisficing threshold and whose expected resource consumption is feasible over the time horizon). Our regret analysis, supported by an LP-duality argument, establishes that SELECTwK attains constant expected satisficing regret when a satisficing policy exists. We further introduce a stronger regret condition that bounds the expected sum of positive reward deficits to the optimal one at each time step, under which SELECTwK achieves a sharper constant bound together with a sub-linear bound in the time horizon. As a complement, SELECTwK still preserves the oracle's sub-linear expected standard regret bound if the satisficing threshold is unattainable. Finally, we establish the oracle conditions and corresponding satisficing regret bound for existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms, and conduct numerical experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory to demonstrate the empirical performance of SELECTwK.

title: Generating pivot Gray codes for spanning arborescences of complete digraphs and split digraphs in constant amortized time
summary: We present the first known efficient algorithm to generate pivot Gray codes for spanning arborescences of complete digraphs, listing all spanning arborescences such that consecutive arborescences differ by reassigning the outgoing edge of exactly one vertex. Our recursive algorithm generates each spanning arborescence in constant amortized time using $O(n^2)$ space. We then extend our algorithm to generate the first known pivot Gray codes for spanning arborescences of split digraphs, achieving constant amortized time per arborescence using $ O(n^2) $ space. Finally, we further generalize our approach to proper interval digraphs. When the arborescences are rooted at the leftmost interval, our algorithm generates the pivot Gray code in constant amortized time per arborescence using $ {O}(n^2) $ space.

title: xCHEM: SDR-Based Multi-Link Channel Emulator for Real-Time Hardware-in-the-Loop Digital-Twin
summary: This paper presents xCHEM, a radio-frequency channel emulator that inserts programmable channels between physical radios using a single NI USRP X4xx software-defined radio. External channel models stream impulse responses to its field-programmable gate array without firmware changes or interruption of signal processing. A streaming datapath implements six independently configurable directional channels across four radio interfaces. Each channel uses a sparse finite impulse response filter whose memory-backed delays decouple delay span from multiplier resources. The real and complex variants support 32 and 16 nonzero taps, respectively, with a maximum delay of 16666.62 ns and 4.069 ns resolution. Coefficient scaling and arithmetic right shifts control attenuation. Hardware measurements show root-mean-square errors of 9.5 ps in delay over the full span and 0.11 dB in attenuation. Multipath delays are recovered within one sample. An FPGA coefficient engine produces tested Doppler shifts from +/-1 Hz to +/-1 MHz with mean frequency errors below 0.032 Hz relative to quantized commands after carrier-offset calibration; at 200 Hz, it reduces the measured near-carrier spur by 53.3 dB compared with 1 kHz host updates.

title: Weighted Score Matching on Bounded Domains: Nonparametric Density Estimation and Interaction Graph Recovery
summary: We study nonparametric density estimation and interaction-graph recovery on bounded product domains using boundary-weighted score matching. In a canonically centered pairwise log-density model, graph edges are determined by bivariate interactions, but penalizing the univariate main effects can induce false edges. We derive the resulting shift in interaction scores and study partially penalized weighted score matching (P-WSM), which leaves main effects unpenalized. At the population level, P-WSM excludes edges between independent subsystems even when the marginal log densities are not represented exactly by the sieve. A nonparametric construction separates partial and joint penalization: throughout a common deterministic tuning interval, P-WSM recovers the graph while joint penalization selects a false edge. We also give growing-dimensional recovery conditions that do not require full-Gram invertibility. For density estimation at fixed dimension, we establish weighted Fisher-divergence rates and, under stronger basis-specific conditions, Kullback-Leibler and Hellinger rates for the normalized estimator. Simulations examine the benefits and limitations of partial penalization. An analysis of bone-marrow signaling data illustrates nonlinear conditional-association estimation.

title: Sparse tensor networks for individual tree diameter estimation in mixed forests
summary: Measurements of tree diameter at breast height (DBH) are fundamental to forest inventories, but manual surveys across entire stands or regions are impractical. UAV-borne laser scanning (ULS) enables scalable automated forest surveys, yet canopy occlusion makes accurate DBH estimation from ULS point clouds non-trivial. Limited stem-level point density of ULS data constrains approaches relying on detailed stem reconstruction, such as Quantitative Structure Models (QSMs) and circle fitting. Empirical machine learning methods based on predefined point cloud metrics are an alternative. New deep learning approaches offer an even more principled solution, allowing models to learn directly from point clouds. Sparse tensor networks have shown particular promise, transforming forestry tasks such as tree species classification. We investigate whether these strengths can be extended to estimate individual tree DBH from ULS data across four mixed-species temperate forest plots in Germany. We further advance existing sparse tensor networks by introducing TreeNext, a lightweight deep learning architecture for direct individual tree parameter estimation from voxelized LiDAR point clouds. We present a fully automated forest inventory pipeline from individual tree instance segmentation to DBH regression, and quantify the impact of segmentation errors by comparing performance on automatically segmented and ground truth instances. TreeNext achieves an $R^2$ of 0.8355 on automatically segmented trees and 0.9380 on ground truth segments, outperforming strong tabular baselines including Random Forest and XGBoost. Segmentation quality emerges as the dominant error source in the automated pipeline. TreeNext proves highly data-efficient, performing well even in small data scenarios. Our findings establish sparse tensor networks as a practical foundation for automated individual tree DBH estimation from ULS.
