title: Learning Latent Fields in Multiobject Tracking
summary: Multiobject tracking using measurements from ar- rays of wireless sensors is a key task in applications ranging from autonomous navigation to public safety. Many existing methods compress raw complex-valued signals into detections or intensity maps during preprocessing, thereby discarding poten- tially relevant information about the objects and the propagation environment. We propose a Bayesian framework for multiobject tracking that relates object states to raw complex-valued signals via a physics-based superpositional model. The model combines a physics-based array manifold, such as radar steering vectors or the replica vectors of matched-field processing, with a latent field. This latent field is a family of context-dependent signal- power distributions that captures the effects of the objects and the propagation environment and is shared across objects and time. It is parameterized by a conditional normalizing flow, which is trained during runtime without labeled data by maximizing an evidence lower bound (ELBO) derived from the Bayesian model. Learning and inference are thus coupled in a sequential framework. We evaluate the method in simulation and in real-world radio and acoustic experiments, with spatial scales ranging from meters to kilometers, and show that it outperforms detection-based methods.

title: Self-normalised change point tests that remain pivotal under non-stationarity
comment: Keywords: Changepoint testing, nonstationarity, temporal dependence, self-normalisation
summary: Self-normalising test statistics for time series circumvent the lag-specification of long-run variance estimators by employing an inconsistent estimator for studentization. This leads to asymptotically pivotal test distributions under stationarity, but not for nonstationary sequences. Focusing on the multiple changepoint problem, we propose an alternative self-normalised test statistic which is asymptotically pivotal even if the noise is nonstationary. Central to our argument are statistical functionals which are invariant under temporal reparametriation, i.e. clock-changes. Simulations show that the proposed procedure is more conservative than competing bootstrap procedures, but considerably more powerful against multiple changes and more reliable in terms of size for highly nonstationary time series in larger samples.

title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
summary:
Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
  We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
  We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything

title: Guidance-Coupled Nullspace Drifting for One-Step Medical Image Reconstruction
summary: Generative reconstruction can recover high-quality images from undersampled acquisitions, but state-of-the-art generative priors commonly rely on iterative sampling. Reducing the number of iterations lowers inference cost but also removes opportunities for progressive distributional refinement, making it difficult to retain image realism without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity. Drift modeling offers an alternative by shifting progressive refinement to training, thereby enabling one-step sampling without an iterative inference trajectory. Existing drifting methods, however, do not account for the imaging operator when modeling distributional drift. We propose DriftRecon, a generative method for one-step medical image reconstruction that performs drifting directly in the nullspace of the imaging operator. DriftRecon uses nullspace-restricted noise to construct training samples and a multiscale generator that incorporates measurement conditioning across resolution levels, with its generated component projected onto the operator nullspace. To control the fidelity--realism trade-off at inference, a conditional guidance parameter continuously steers the same generator between measurement-conditioned and unconditional generation. We derive a guidance-dependent similarity-kernel temperature schedule that preserves the guidance-weighted mass receiving strengthened supervision, thereby progressively localizing drift interactions as guidance increases to limit the associated loss of reconstruction fidelity. Experiments in sparse-view CT and accelerated MRI reconstruction show that DriftRecon outperforms established generative reconstruction methods and recent drifting models while producing reconstructions in a single forward pass.

title: Nonlinear Sufficient Dimension Reduction for Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments
summary: Causal inference with continuous treatments requires estimating nuisance functions to adjust for the potentially high-dimensional confounder, but nonparametric estimation of these functions is severely hampered by the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we propose a nonlinear sufficient dimension reduction framework to construct low-dimensional sufficient confounders to preserve the unbiasedness of the treatment effect. We estimate the causal effect by combining the generalized Sliced Inverse Regression with the inverse probability weighting, outcome regression, and augmented inverse probability weighting, respectively. We further establish the convergence rates of the first two estimators and derive the asymptotic distributions of the third. Our theoretical results show that, compared to estimators based on the full covariates, dimension reduction yields faster convergence rates and weaker rate conditions without inflating the asymptotic variance. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed estimators improve finite-sample performance over their counterparts without dimension reduction, particularly when the original covariate dimension is high. These results demonstrate that sufficient dimension reduction provides a flexible approach to mitigating the curse of dimensionality in causal inference with continuous treatments.

title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models
summary: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.

title: Waveform Bandwidth and Frequency Diversity in FDA-MIMO Range-Angle Estimation: A CRLB Perspective
summary: Frequency-diverse array multiple-input multiple-output (FDA-MIMO) radar introduces range-dependent phase diversity through element-dependent carrier-frequency offsets, in addition to the delay information carried by transmitted waveforms. This paper develops a bandwidth-aware Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) framework to characterize how these two mechanisms jointly affect range-angle estimation. Starting from a Nyquist-rate sampled observation model that retains waveform delays and FDA frequency offsets, we derive an equivalent Fisher information matrix (EFIM) after eliminating an unknown quasi-static complex scattering coefficient as a nuisance parameter. We derive closed-form CRLB approximations that reveal the interplay between waveform root-mean-square (RMS) bandwidth and FDA frequency diversity. A three-factor decomposition of the squared normalized cross-information further characterizes range-angle coupling. Results show that when increased independently, both waveform RMS bandwidth and FDA frequency diversity reduce the range CRLB, but FDA frequency diversity increases the angle CRLB at fixed nonzero waveform bandwidth, whereas waveform RMS bandwidth reduces it. Additionally, under a fixed aggregate spectral budget, the range CRLB exhibits an interior maximum, whereas the angle CRLB increases monotonically with the FDA spectral-allocation fraction. Numerical results corroborate the closed-form approximations and the predicted trends.

title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System
summary: Under Major League Baseball's automated ball-strike (ABS) challenge system, players must weigh the value of overturning a call against the risk of losing a challenge they may need later. We develop a policy that values an overturn through its effect on expected runs, accounting for the count, outs, and runners on base. Using pitch tracking and game records, we reconstruct challenge opportunities, including calls that players let stand. A Bayesian model represents players' imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions. Dynamic programming compares the expected gain with the future cost of losing a challenge, accounting for the stage of the game, the number of challenges remaining, and opportunities on both offense and defense. We develop the policy using games before the 2026 All-Star break and evaluate it without refitting on 983 games played afterward. Along the recorded sequence of opportunities, the policy recovers 0.536 modeled correction runs per game across both teams, compared with 0.452 under observed decisions, an improvement of 18.5%. The gain is 0.084 runs per game, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.065, 0.103]. The policy makes more challenges and recovers more value per successful review despite a lower overturn rate. These results show why overturn rate alone can be a misleading measure of challenge strategy.

title: The Interference-Conjugate Transform: The Tightest Interference-Linear Surrogate for Power Control, Scheduling and Beamforming in Wireless Networks
summary: Closed-form fractional programming (FP), weighted MMSE (WMMSE), and the 2026 surrogate-enhanced methods SEFP and XMMSE all maximize the weighted sum rate by iteratively maximizing a surrogate linear in the interference power. We show that this family admits a unique best member: the interference-conjugate transform (ICT), which replaces each rate term $\log(1+a/b)$ by $\max_{κ\ge0}[Ω(κa)-κb]$, where $Ω$ is the closed-form partial convex conjugate of the rate in the interference variable and the optimal multiplier is the interference price $a/(b(a+b))$. We prove that, for any fixed price, $Ω(κ\,\cdot)$ is the pointwise largest own-signal function compatible with a valid interference-linear lower bound, and that tightness at an anchor forces the price. Hence all four benchmark surrogates, which share this price and differ only in their own-signal term, are dominated pointwise by ICT. At SINR $γ$, the benchmarks' own-signal curvature exceeds the true curvature by factors behaving as $γ/2$ (FP/WMMSE) and $(\logγ)/2$ (SEFP/XMMSE), against $1+1/(γ(γ+2))$ for ICT, and this ordering carries over to the certified ascent per iteration and the asymptotic linear convergence rate. ICT yields closed-form updates at the benchmarks' per-iteration cost for single-antenna power control, uplink joint scheduling and power control, and multi-cell MISO beamforming, and the first solver-free algorithm for sum-least-$q$th-percentile rate maximization, via a $K$-dimensional convex dual with closed-form gradient and Hessian and a certified duality gap. In uplink scheduling, ICT improves proportional-fairness utility over FP by +7.03 and over SEFP by +3.35 (60/60 drops) using 18.7 iterations per slot vs. 49.7 and 38.0; in MISO beamforming with $M=8$, it reaches 99.9% of its final value in a median of 9 iterations vs. 16 (XMMSE) and 1160 (FP/WMMSE).

title: Stability-Performance Trade-off in Maritime Integrated Sensing, Communication, and Computation: A Lyapunov-Guided Dual-Timescale Hierarchical RL Approach
summary: Driven by the ever-growing demand for intelligent maritime services, cooperative unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned surface vehicle (USV) operations, together with wireless integrated sensing, communication, and computation (ISCC), have become pivotal in maritime environments. However, the distinctive maritime environment precludes a direct application of terrestrial ISCC models, while sensing, communication, and computation compete for the same spatio-temporal resources, thus yielding inherent performance trade-offs that become particularly severe in resource-constrained ocean scenarios. To address these issues, we investigate an ISCC system in which multiple UAVs detect targets at the sea surface and partially offload the collected data to a USV for cooperative processing. Characterizing the maritime-specific environment impairments, we incorporate sea clutter and wave-induced USV roll motion into the sensing and communication models, respectively. Moreover, we introduce data queueing models at both the UAVs and the USV to capture the dynamic coupling among sensing-data generation, wireless offloading, and computation execution. The optimization objective is to minimize the long-term average system energy consumption by jointly optimizing UAV-target association, UAV trajectories, beamforming, time allocation, offloading ratios, and computation resource allocation. Given that these decisions differ in update frequency and time sensitivity, we propose a Lyapunov-guided dual-timescale hierarchical soft actor-critic (LTH-SAC) framework, which transforms the long-term problem into a sequence of queue-aware online subproblems and coordinates optimization across the two timescales. Simulation results verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework and demonstrate its capability to balance the stability-performance trade-off among sensing, communication, and computation.

title: What's Old Is New: Improved Learning from Small-Group Tutorials
comment: 16 pages, 2 tables. Code and synthetic data: https://github.com/dlsun/tutorials
summary: The ubiquity of Large Language Models poses a challenge to student learning in homework-based college courses, where access to easy homework answers devalues the intended productive struggle. To address this concern, we propose Oxbridge-style weekly tutorials, where students present homework problems without notes in a small group with an instructor or TA. We conducted a randomized experiment in an introductory probability class to evaluate the effectiveness of tutorials, finding a significant positive effect of tutorial enrollment on exam grades. We discuss the implementation, challenges, and opportunities in this style of course design.

title: Spokes, not a Ring: Revisiting the Weekday Manifold in Language Models
summary: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.

title: Sensing Fast and Distant Targets in Overspread Channels with Zak-OTFS and Modular Arithmetic
summary: Delay-Doppler (DD) modulations, such as Zak-transform-based orthogonal time frequency space (Zak-OTFS) modulation, represent the channel as a sparse set of delay and Doppler shifts, which makes them well suited for radar sensing. Sensing with a single DD frame, however, is unambiguous only when the channel spread factor, i.e., the product of the delay and Doppler spreads, is below one. Long-range mobility scenarios, including drones, airplanes, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites, and underwater acoustic links, typically violate this crystallization condition, so that a single frame aliases the target delays, Doppler shifts, or both. Existing methods add a time-frequency pilot to a conventional DD frame and resolve the aliasing in only one dimension. We propose a frame design that combines multiple DD bases with different delay and Doppler periods, which together cover an overspread channel, on the same bandwidth and frame size. For two frames, we show that modular arithmetic on the wrapped peak positions uniquely recovers each target by pairing the peaks through their common projection and their gains, and we derive the condition under which this pairing is ambiguous. We implement the design with two superimposed Zak-OTFS frames and propose two receivers: dual-frame sensing (DS), which performs the joint detection directly, and DS with cross-pilot cancellation (DS-XC), which additionally cancels the cross-pilot interference, re-estimates the gains by joint least squares, and removes ghost targets. Both receivers keep a detection rate close to one as the spread factor grows, and DS-XC also achieves the lowest false-alarm rate and channel normalized mean squared error (NMSE). In a 100 km drone scenario, DS-XC detects 98% of the targets, compared with 81% for the best baseline, with a complexity that grows near-linearly with the time-bandwidth product for a fixed number of targets.

title: The Cost of Working Memory in Streaming Mean Estimation
summary: A streaming estimator must compute from the evidence that fits in memory. We determine when storing an accurate mean is easier than computing it. For Gaussian mean estimation over the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we establish the minimax rate under squared error with $K$ persistent states, a known horizon, and a public time index: $\min\{1, K^{-2/d}+\frac{d}{n} (1+\frac{\log(ed)}{1+(\log K)/d})\}$. Unrestricted computation followed by $K$-level encoding has rate $\min\{1,d/n+K^{-2/d}\}$. At a fixed sufficiently small error, statistically optimal sample size therefore requires order $d\log d$ working bits, while order $d$ bits suffice to store the answer. The lower bound tracks repeated state compression through an entropy potential obtained by Gaussian smoothing. A matching construction combines a multiscale modular counter with workspace reused across coordinate groups. In one dimension, it attains the terminal rate $n^{-1}+K^{-2}$. Any fixed confidence requirement that the realized loss not exceed the zero baseline preserves these rates. Increasing confidence creates a further memory requirement: at fixed nontrivial risk in every fixed dimension, failure probability $e^{-γn}$ requires and permits order $\log n$ working states for sufficiently small fixed $γ>0$. In the scalar problem, a fixed terminal alphabet suffices under the same protection. These bounds separate the memory needed to represent an answer from the memory needed to accumulate evidence and validate a decision.

title: Structured Security Explanations for Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection
summary:
Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection.
  We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention.
  We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.

title: Turning Multipath into Positioning Information: Persistent Electromagnetic-Twin DoA Localization
summary: Reflected paths can support localization when line-of-sight (LoS) links are blocked, but their usefulness depends on how accurately the stored model predicts their directions. This paper develops electromagnetic-twin (ET) direction-of-arrival (DoA) localization with a persistent, physically calibrated path-angle field. A nominal floor plan supplies virtual-path geometry, and sparse reference probes at known positions learn a compact directional correction. Field order and regularization are selected from calibration data alone. For each user, unordered DoAs are processed by joint position estimation and one-to-one path association, using assignment-aware multistart search and robust Gauss--Newton refinement. New trusted probes update the stored correction through recursive least squares (RLS), without reprocessing all previous measurements. The analysis establishes calibration rank conditions, objective descent, and conditional information gains from reflected paths, while also distinguishing the decay of initialization bias from the convergence of localization error. Synthetic experiments use 500 queries per operating point. At 50% LoS blockage and $1.5^\circ$ DoA error, the calibrated ET achieves 0.39 m root-mean-square error, versus 0.55 m for nominal geometry. After a wall change, its final error is 0.43 m, versus 0.63 m for a frozen calibrated map. Equal-evidence comparisons show competitive calibrated alternatives and faster abrupt-change recovery with sliding-window updates than with the configured RLS. The results support reusable directional calibration, not a universally superior map or update rule, and validation is limited to synthetic first-order reflections with trusted calibration labels.

title: TabCUQ: Context-Uncertainty Quantification for Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular foundation models use in-context learning to estimate conditional expected outcomes and average treatment effects for specific groups of individuals. Using these estimates to guide scientific decisions requires reliable uncertainty quantification. The challenge is to account simultaneously for two sources of uncertainty: limited-context bias and context variation arising from the small labeled sample supplied at inference. Predictive spread does not directly quantify both sources of uncertainty, and we observe that the ordinary bootstrap may substantially overestimate context variation, whereas subsampling may underestimate it. We introduce TabCUQ, a perturbation-based framework that injects noise into observed outcomes and applies the foundation model to the perturbed contexts. TabCUQ estimates context variation using wild-bootstrap dispersion and accounts for limited-context bias using the maximum deviation between perturbed and original estimates. For a kernel-regression analogue whose estimation error admits an exact decomposition into these two components, we show that our framework provides asymptotically valid pointwise coverage. In simulations, TabCUQ substantially improves coverage, with average interval widths typically about twice those of an oracle bias-aware benchmark. Across seven real-world tasks, it also improves coverage of reference functions learned from much larger samples.

title: DexSuite: An All-in-One Framework for Dexterous Manipulation Across Arms, Hands, and Tasks
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://dexsuiteorg.github.io
summary: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at https://dexsuiteorg.github.io

title: Array-Agnostic High-Order Ambisonics Encoding via Diffusion Posterior Sampling
summary: Ambisonics provides a device-independent representation of three-dimensional sound fields; however, extracting these coefficients from practical microphone array recordings remains strongly dependent on array geometry, acoustic transfer functions, and spatial sampling resolution. This pipeline is typically divided into two distinct tasks: encoding, which entails reconstructing the physically resolvable spatial components, and upscaling, which requires generating higher-order coefficients. Model-based approaches often fail on irregular arrays due to ill-conditioned transfer matrices, whereas conventional neural encoders remain strictly tied to the specific acquisition setup seen during training. Furthermore, existing upscaling methods usually assume ideal low-order inputs, ignoring device-specific array artifacts. We present ADEUPS, a unified framework that couples an array-independent Ambisonic diffusion prior with an explicit physical acquisition model during inference, enabling zero-shot encoding and upscaling across diverse array configurations. We train our prior using an order-masking strategy and perform inference via score blending, which we demonstrate to be crucial for solving the underlying inverse problem. Through extensive numerical evaluations across various array geometries, we show that ADEUPS consistently outperforms task- and array-specific baselines. Finally, we conduct subjective listening tests to confirm the perceptual effectiveness of our approach.

title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response
summary: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies -- spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) -- against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.

title: An Empirical Study of Wrist-Target Construction and Joint-Angle Limits in Humanoid Arm Retargeting
summary: Motion retargeting maps a demonstrated human movement onto a robot to compute its joint motion. This study examines how the construction of the desired wrist position affects whether computed arm joint angles reach their permitted limits on a Unitree H1-2. A reconstructed target is formed from demonstrated arm directions and robot segment lengths, so its shoulder-to-wrist distance depends on the demonstrated angle between the segments even when no posture-matching preference is applied. A reach-normalized target retains that direction while rescaling the distance, using the same processed demonstrations and the same joint-angle method. Across a forward-reach sweep the reconstructed target places a joint angle at a bound in 10 of 20 repetitions and the reach-normalized target in none. Across 25 recordings from one participant the corresponding counts are 8 and 6 on the reaching arm and 14 and 5 on the supporting arm, and a second participant repeats the bricklaying and lifting comparison. In hardware replay a joint is commanded to a bound in 12 of 16 direction-matching arm-records and in none of the 16 normalized records, and within the eligible records both tracking error and executed torque at those frames exceed their values elsewhere in the same run. Cross-body reach and arm-to-arm clearance identify limits of radial adjustment. The findings support treating target construction and posture matching as separate retargeting decisions, and evaluating both alongside the wrist positions and clearance that manipulation requires.

title: An Efficient SIM Beamforming Scheme Based on Physical-Empowered Projected Gradient
summary: Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces (SIMs) have emerged as a promising technology for next-generation wireless systems. Especially in multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems, it has the potential to realize complicated wave-domain transformations with low hardware costs and energy consumption. However, SIM-assisted MIMO systems face two major challenges in channel estimation and beamforming. As the SIM elements do not have the signal processing capability, channel estimation can only be conducted in an indirect manner, which makes it challenging. Moreover, the precoding optimization after channel estimation is non-convex and also difficult. Targeting these issues, we exploit the time-division duplex (TDD) channel reciprocity to calculate the gradient backpropagation in an over-the-air manner. Based on this structure, we propose a gradient-based optimization framework that optimizes beamforming without explicitly estimating the SIM--UE channel. The proposed method, namely the physical projected gradient descent (P2GD) method, optimizes the achievable sum rate while incorporating zero-forcing (ZF) constraints. Based on the method of incorporating the ZF restriction, we propose two variations of P2GD, namely user equipment (UE)-P2GD and base station (BS)-P2GD. We also provide a theoretical convergence analysis and projected gradient techniques to ensure physical feasibility. Simulation results show that the proposed approach can achieve suboptimal beamforming in the multi-user system within a small number of over-the-air iterations, using a per-direction signaling budget below the pilot cost of explicit SIM--UE channel estimation. The proposed method provides a low-overhead beamforming scheme for SIM systems without explicit SIM--UE channel estimation.

title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
summary: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $Θ\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(Θ)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(Θ)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $Θ$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $Θ$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $Θ$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $Θ$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.

authors: Domingos Fortunato P. F. da Silva
Wouter A. J. Van den Broeck
title: 3Dtrees.earth: community research infrastructure for tree and forest analysis using close-range LiDAR data
summary: From individual trees to forest stands, three-dimensional structure shapes carbon, water, and energy flows, habitat conditions, and resource availability. Yet tree and forest structural attributes remain difficult to assess consistently across space and time. Close-range LiDAR (light detection and ranging) records detailed 3D structure from branches and trees to forest plots, including trees outside forests. However, broader reuse is constrained when data, acquisition context, processing, computation, and access conditions are maintained separately. We present 3Dtrees.earth, an operational community research infrastructure that brings close-range LiDAR datasets, analysis tools, and computing resources together while linking original observations to their metadata and processing outputs. As of 23 October 2026, the platform comprised 2,760 datasets, including 2,481 publicly visible datasets. These point cloud datasets span 46 countries on all six inhabited continents and include terrestrial, mobile, and uncrewed aerial laser scanning. Users can contribute and discover datasets, run standardized processing workflows on shared computing infrastructure, inspect point clouds and model predictions in the browser, and access data and processing outputs together with citation information. Workflows combine rule-based and machine-learning methods, with tools updated as methods advance. Outputs include raster products, individual-tree and semantic segmentation, and tree- and stand-level metrics. Original point clouds and processing records are retained, enabling reprocessing with improved tools while preserving provenance. With broader coverage, curation, and validation, this shared resource could extend individual surveys into a basis for model evaluation and benchmarking, cross-site synthesis, calibration and validation of larger-scale Earth observation products, and macroecological analysis.

title: Tracking analysis of compressed-communication distributed adaptive estimation for time-varying parameters
summary: This paper studies the problem of distributed time-varying parameter tracking over communication-constrained networks. To mitigate the accumulation of induced compression errors across the network, we propose a differentially compressed distributed least mean squares (LMS) algorithm.In the proposed scheme, each sensor updates a local auxiliary state recursively based on the compressed difference between the current parameter estimate and the previous auxiliary state, and then transmits only this compressed difference to its neighbors for auxiliary-state reconstruction. This differential recursion mechanism helps control the accumulation of compression errors and accommodates a general class of randomized compressors including randomized quantizers and sparsifiers.We establish the mean-square boundedness and explicit steady-state tracking-error bound under a cooperative excitation condition on stochastic regression vectors, which captures both temporal and spatial information to reflect the joint excitation effect of sensors.Notably, our stability analysis requires neither temporal independence nor stationarity of regressors, nor persistent excitation at individual nodes, thereby accommodating correlated and nonstationary signals from stochastic feedback systems. Numerical simulations demonstrate the theoretical results under correlated and non-stationary regression data.

title: Variational Bayes for Variable Selection with Adaptive Sharing across Populations and Responses
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Supplementary material (54 pages) is available as an ancillary PDF
summary: We propose a variational Bayesian framework for variable selection with multiple responses across heterogeneous populations. The prior dependence among the inclusion indicators allows variable-selection information to be shared at different levels across populations and responses, while regression coefficients remain population- and response-specific. When the appropriate sharing structure is unknown, a data-driven rule adaptively determines the scope of information sharing from marginal association evidence. The resulting variational algorithm is computationally scalable and can be implemented using either individual-level or summary data. Under regularity conditions, we establish selection consistency and convergence properties of the variational parameters at fixed iterations of the algorithm for fixed dimension case. In high dimensions, we establish model-selection consistency and coefficient contraction in both $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms. Simulation studies show competitive variable selection performance and demonstrate the potential gains from joint analysis. We further illustrate the summary-data implementation using genome-wide association summary statistics from the 2021 Global Lipids Genetics Consortium study for four lipid traits across five populations.

title: New Election, Same Old Story: How Tropes Form a Grammar of Election Rumors
summary: Recent elections in the United States have seen online rumors become a regular feature of election discourse as voters and election officials work to navigate a sea of digitally spread claims and propaganda. For the uninitiated, these rumors can feel overwhelming and random, sowing doubt about the integrity and legitimacy of recent elections. In this paper, we reviewed and qualitatively coded a large dataset of 590 election rumors collected during the the 2020 and 2022 national elections. We found that there are tropes that recur time and time again in election rumors, highlighting how these rumors are not as random as they may first appear. We make two primary contributions in this work: first, we introduce a hierarchical framework that structures observed tropes in three tiers (Meta-category, Meso-trope, and Micro-trope). Second, combining the framework with our coded data, we identify a visible grammar of election rumors, highlighting how in the majority of cases a rumor contains an Actor, and Object, and an Action, with optional grammatical components of Suggested Remedies and Scene & Setting. The framework and grammar can be used by other researchers to act as the underlying information architecture of analyses examining similar rumors, enabling the rapid identification, analysis, and prediction of election rumors.

title: Compound Climate Risk-Aware Electricity Dispatch: Trajectory-Based Modeling for Power System Resilience
summary: In recent decades, emerging compound hazards in a changing climate have increasingly threatened power system resilience and posed new challenges to electricity dispatch. Conventional Value-at-Risk (VaR)-based risk-aware dispatch provides a tractable means of managing stochastic net demand deviations caused by distribution feeder outages. However, when applied to temporally compounding events such as tropical cyclone (TC)--blackout--heatwave, conventional net demand risk formulations may assign similar risk levels to a brief outage and an outage with the same instantaneous net demand impact that persists into a subsequent hazard, despite their different requirements for sustained operational flexibility. Moreover, directly incorporating compound risk into electricity dispatch models faces a structural mismatch: the risk is defined by the joint distribution of feeder restoration and subsequent hazards over exponentially many joint states, whereas dispatch models require risk formulations that are tractable in the scheduling decisions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a compound climate risk-aware dispatch framework with a trajectory-based compound risk model, which defines the loss on operating deviations determined by entire feeder connection trajectories, parameterized by uncertain restoration times and coupled with subsequent hazards. Analytical moment-generating functions and equivalent exponential-cone reformulations provide a compact representation of the resulting risk constraints, preserving the relevant dependencies without explicit joint-state enumeration. By leveraging a physics-based spatiotemporal TC--blackout--heatwave hazard model, case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with real-world time-series power outage data from Puerto Rico, including data collected during Hurricane Fiona in 2022.

title: Generalized Posterior Calibration via Infinitesimal-Jackknife Variance Matching
summary: Generalized posteriors update a prior through an exponential transformation of empirical loss rather than a conventional likelihood, with a learning rate controlling posterior concentration. Their credible intervals may have incorrect frequentist coverage because posterior dispersion need not reflect sampling variability. We propose infinitesimal-jackknife variance matching (IJVM), a computationally efficient method for selecting the learning rate for a prespecified scalar functional. IJVM matches the functional's posterior variance to an infinitesimal-jackknife estimate of the sampling variance of its posterior mean, computed from posterior covariances with observation-level losses. A multiplicative one-step update requires one pilot posterior fit and a second fit for inference, avoiding explicit estimation of loss Hessians or gradient covariance matrices and repeated bootstrap posterior fitting. Under suitable regularity and Monte Carlo accuracy conditions, we establish consistency of the selected rate for the functional-specific first-order calibration target. With additional sampling and posterior-quantile assumptions, the resulting credible intervals achieve asymptotically nominal frequentist coverage. Simulations involving homoscedastic and heteroscedastic regression and hinge-loss classification show that one-step IJVM achieves coverage near the nominal 95% level, with interval lengths comparable to bootstrap-based generalized posterior calibration but substantially fewer posterior fits. Additional updates offer little improvement.

title: TACOS: Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision for Visual Footstep Planning
summary: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/TACOS.

title: Anchor-Free Range-Free 3D IoT Localization in Buried Environments with Connectivity-Informed Power Selection and Temporal Refinement
summary: In underground and surface mines, wireless Internet-of- Things (IoT) tags deployed with ore or muck loads can support material and grade tracking after burial, when conventional ranging and surveyed localization infrastructure may be unavailable. Building on the three-dimensional Pro- traction Technique (3D-PT), this paper introduces 3D-PT with Power Selection (3D-PT-PS), which selects informative transmit-power levels from binary pilot measurements, and 3D-PT-PS with Temporal Refinement (3D-PT-PST), which incorporates recorded load-deposition times as weak, non- metric cues. Both methods are anchor-free and range-free and require no RSSI, measured ranges, surveyed anchors, pile dimensions, or material parameters. Monte Carlo simulations evaluate different pile sizes and tag densities. In a 5000-t crusher-pocket scenario with 125 tags, 3D-PT-PST achieves 6.12% mean NRMSE and 2.20 m 3D RMSE, reducing mean NRMSE by 13.5% relative to 3D-PT-PS and by 43.6% and 69.1% relative to calibrated MDS-MAP(P) and CATL, respectively. These results show that connectivity and timing provide complementary information.

title: Bayes-Consistent Losses for Adaptive Inference in Classification
summary: Adaptive inference systems balance accuracy and inference cost by routing inputs to models with varying capabilities. Although jointly training models and routers is empirically more sample-efficient than training them separately, principled losses for joint training remain underexplored. We address this gap in a classification setting by proposing cost-sensitive hinge losses for jointly training classifiers with single-stage or cascade routers. Single-stage routers directly select a model per input, whereas cascade routers sequentially decide at each stage whether to predict with the current model or defer to the next stage, which uses a more accurate but more costly model. For both settings, we prove linear calibration bounds establishing Bayes consistency: minimizing the hinge risk recovers the Bayes-optimal risk under the target cost-sensitive zero-one loss. Moreover, since routers can require more labeled data to train than classifiers, we propose a novel post-training prediction-powered inference (PPI) procedure that uses unlabeled data to refine a trained single-stage router. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed hinge losses are effective for joint training and that PPI can correct routing errors when labeled data is scarce.

title: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs
summary: LLM agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in checks derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge. Yet a checker can be wrong as well: it can miss errors, and it can flag correct answers and push the agent into "fixing" them. Whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as such a judge, and how it compares with an ontology an LLM writes or a schema mined from the data, is unknown. We make the checker itself the object of study. Across curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies, used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, and across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly $10^{9}$ triples, we account for what ontology-derived checks catch and what they wrongly flag. We show how each source trades caught errors against false alarms, how a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, which errors structural checks miss, and whether combining sources or giving the agent the checker's specific feedback pays off. On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either an ontology derived from the data or one an LLM derives from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. On real agent answers, its flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.

title: BEVLight: Generalizable Traffic Signal Control from UAV Bird's-Eye Views
summary: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.

title: Fast rates for the classification of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck paths
summary: In binary classification problems, plug-in classifiers can sometimes achieve faster excess risk rates than the underlying estimation rate. In this work, we study a supervised classification problem based on repeated independent observations of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck paths, with both time-homogeneous and time-inhomogeneous drifts. We show that, under a suitable separation condition on the class-dependent drifts, a plug-in classifier attains an excess risk of quadratic order in the corresponding parametric or nonparametric estimation error. The theoretical approach utilizes the Wiener chaos representation and spectral theory to characterize the log-likelihood ratio as a quadratic form of Gaussian random variables, enabling a precise analysis of margin behaviour and deviation results. This extends the fast-rate results from classification problems with linear discriminant models and Gaussian white noise models to dynamical diffusion systems with Gaussian structure.

title: ConfluxServe: Reconciling Resource Utilization and Parallelism Efficiency across Prefill and Decode in LLM Serving
summary:
Prefill and decode are complementary in resource usage, but often divergent in parallelism preferences. Executing the two phases separately preserves their preferred parallelism but leaves complementary resources underutilized, while co-batching improves utilization but often requires a uniform parallel configuration that hurts execution efficiency.
  To resolve this utilization-efficiency dilemma, we propose Conflux Parallelism (XP), a parallel execution abstraction that co-executes prefill and decode with different parallelism within the same batch. Conflux Parallelism exploits operator-level Transformer structure to construct a heterogeneous execution path with different batching and parallelism strategies across operators, combining the best of co-batching and phase-specific execution. Building on Conflux Parallelism, we design ConfluxServe, an SLO-aware serving system that maximizes cluster goodput under TTFT and TBT constraints. Evaluation on production workloads shows that ConfluxServe improves serving goodput by 1.26-1.62x over the strongest baselines.

title: LLM eBay: A Simple and Truthful Marketplace for Fine-Tuned LLMs Trading
summary: Personalized fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) enhances user experience but incurs substantial computational costs. Recent studies show that initializing training from a style-similar fine-tuned model reduces adaptation overhead, turning such checkpoints into reusable, tradable assets. A marketplace for these checkpoints, however, faces information asymmetry: sellers may misreport a checkpoint's style, while buyers cannot verify its usefulness before purchase, which invites adverse selection. We introduce LLM eBay, a simple single-round marketplace for trading fine-tuned LLMs. Sellers are paid per purchase at a posted price, and a truncated quadratic proper scoring rule adjusts each payment according to how well the seller's style report agrees with a style signal that the platform measures by generating text on hidden prompts. We show that the score elicits the verifier's expected signal, characterize exactly when truthful reporting is a seller best response under per-purchase demand, and bound the downside risk from noisy verification. In an end-to-end study with real LoRA checkpoints on two base models and three buyer tasks, LLM eBay reduces measured convergence steps by 8.5\% relative to retrieval over self-reported style (95\% CI [1.0\%, 15.9\%]). In model-based market simulations built on a measured style-to-cost relationship, it cuts style-claim error by 96.5\% (from 0.424 to 0.015), recovers 96.3\% of Oracle welfare, saves 72.4\% of the cost of fine-tuning from the base model, and keeps all providers profitable in the default setting.

title: Reference-based multiple imputation for longitudinal bounded discrete outcomes
summary: Reference-based multiple imputation has been developed for binary and ordinal responses. We develop a parsimonious formulation for longitudinal bounded scores and counts that preserves their finite integer support and gives partial and complete reference borrowing an explicit distributional interpretation. Discrete Kumaraswamy margins provide closed-form cumulative distribution and quantile functions, simplifying fitting and imputation under a Gaussian copula. Borrowing is defined through a regression model indexed by a smooth median anchor, allowing continuation under the assigned treatment, partial borrowing, or jump to reference after a specified trigger. With shapes shared across arms, complete borrowing replaces the active marginal distribution with the reference distribution at the same visit and covariate values, while conditional imputations remain informed by retained outcomes. Bayesian estimation uses latent variable augmentation, and all sensitivity rules share one fitted posterior. Completed datasets are analyzed using a beta-binomial random intercept model, with treatment comparisons expressed as standardized mean score differences. Simulations assess parameter recovery and imputation followed by analysis. An application to depression scores illustrates attenuation of the treatment benefit at the final visit as borrowing increases, with confidence intervals including zero under all rules.

title: GOFish: Full Field-of-View Gaussian Splatting and Mesh Extraction
summary: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360° cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180° and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180°, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200° FIORD and 205° FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.

title: Limit Theorems and Optimal Policies for Flock Flight through Poisson Forests
summary: Inspired by birds flying through cluttered environments, Karaman and Frazzoli showed that high-speed flight through an ergodic random forest exhibits an ultimate speed limit: above a critical speed, almost surely no infinite collision-free trajectory exists for a single bird. This paper formulates a corresponding bulk-transport problem for many birds. We construct an explicit directed corridor network in a Poisson disk forest and impose a common temporal headway at its waypoints. The maximum current equals a minimum vertex-cut capacity and is achieved by repeated flight along vertex-disjoint paths. The same schedule maximizes completed traversals at every finite horizon, with constant forward speed and no internal waiting. For a forest belt of fixed depth, exact transverse superadditivity yields an almost-sure deterministic current-density limit. A uniform shape theorem for an asymmetric planar dual identifies the current when depth and width grow together. For diverging depth bounded by a constant times width, this current equals the width-first, depth-second limit and is independent of the positive aspect ratio. When diagonal corridors are available, bulk current is positive at sufficiently low obstacle intensity and zero at sufficiently high intensity. For stochastic demand, an upstream admission queue is stable at every rate below the finite-network capacity.

title: The information geometry of the Sinkhorn divergence on a Hilbert manifold
summary: The Sinkhorn divergence, the debiased entropic optimal transport cost, determines a metric tensor on probability measures defined along curves, due to Lavenant et al. We construct a real-analytic Hilbert manifold of measures, the smooth stratum, on which this tensor is a weak Riemannian metric, and we continue Eguchi's construction of a geometry from a divergence to the third order. The stratum consists of the measures with a positive Sobolev density on a closed Riemannian manifold, and the strata form a scale whose intersection is the Fréchet manifold of smooth positive densities of Ay. Following it, we characterize the metric through the gradients of mean values: its cotangent form is a spectral reweighting of the Dirichlet form of a Markov chain, so the metric is of the same kind as the Fisher-Rao and the Otto metric, and on the stratum it is bounded by a multiple of the Fisher-Rao metric (but not conversely). At third order, the Sinkhorn divergence is self-dual: both connection forms of Eguchi's construction coincide with the Levi-Civita form of the metric, and the cubic tensor vanishes, as a consequence of the transposition symmetry of the transport problem. On every stratum, the Levi-Civita form is represented, so the stratum has a real-analytic Levi-Civita connection, which on the Fréchet manifold is the connection of Ay and Schwachhöfer.

title: Responsible Quantum Machine Learning for Medical Imaging: A Fairness Audit Across Sensitive Subgroups
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly explored for medical classification, yet its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria remains understudied. We present an empirical fairness audit of classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging, assuming QML is not inherently fair. Two scenarios are evaluated: dermatological lesions on DDI (sensitive attribute: Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (sensitive attribute: age group). Using ResNet-18 embeddings, we train SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN under a baseline and three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined. Foundation models (PanDerm, EVA-X) serve as external references. Quantum classifiers may achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities. Since a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, each mitigation is also tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin relative to its baseline. Under this criterion, several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performed best and approached PanDerm in the performance/fairness trade-off; on CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieved the highest aggregate performance but increased disparity, and EVA-X remained stronger. Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation; we claim no quantum advantage.

title: Evaluating Generalization and Long-Term Stability of Smartwatch-Based Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring
comment: Accepted by the 2026 IEEE EMBS International Conference on Biomedical and Health Informatics (BHI 2026)
summary: Smartwatch-based cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is a promising low-burden solution for long-term cardiovascular management, but practical deployment remains constrained by model complexity, uncertain cross-dataset generalization, and insufficient evidence on long-term tracking stability. This study presents an efficient Signal-Context Gated Fusion Network (SCGBPNet) for cuffless BP estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. SCGBPNet integrates signal-level representations through self-attention and further incorporates subject-specific contextual information via a compact gated fusion module. On Aurora-BP, SCGBPNet achieved SBP/DBP mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.08/4.90 mmHg, compared with 6.44/4.89 mmHg under within-dataset validation on the private smartwatch dataset, indicating a modest within-dataset discrepancy. Cross-dataset transfer from Aurora-BP to the smartwatch dataset increased the MAEs to 8.98/6.47 mmHg, demonstrating substantial cross-dataset degradation. For long-term stability, the proposed method showed low week-to-week performance variation and a low daily decay rate, indicating good stability over a follow-up period of more than one month. Nevertheless, estimation accuracy deteriorated when BP deviated substantially from an individual's baseline. These findings indicate that favorable aggregate MAE alone should not be interpreted as evidence of deployment-ready performance. More systematic and stratified evaluation across dataset settings, BP ranges, and baseline-deviation levels is needed to assess the practical reliability of smartwatch-based cuffless BP monitoring.

title: Probabilistic Meshless Methods on Manifolds
summary: Probabilistic meshless methods solve partial differential equations (PDEs) by placing a Gaussian process prior on the solution and conditioning it on the PDE at a finite set of collocation nodes. The posterior provides both an approximation of the solution and a Bayesian quantification of its error. While these methods are well established on Euclidean domains, their extension to manifolds lacks, to our knowledge, any convergence analysis. We extend them to compact manifolds and study their convergence in two settings. First, for known manifolds whose Laplace-Beltrami eigenpairs are available, the prior can be evaluated exactly, but the PDE operator generally cannot be applied to it in closed form. We replace this operator by a standard generalized finite difference discretization on a point cloud sampled from the manifold, and show that the resulting method is consistent at the points of the cloud, at a rate governed by their fill distance. Second, for implicit manifolds, known only through a point cloud, both the prior and the operator must be approximated. We propose a new generalized finite difference scheme with a free stencil radius, and show that it retains the consistency of the standard construction while controlling the growth of its coefficients, and that an appropriate radius yields uniform convergence of the discrete Gram matrix. In both settings, we derive error bounds for the posterior mean which separate the collocation error intrinsic to the method from the error due to approximating the operator and, for implicit manifolds, the prior. Experiments on the circle, the sphere and the flat torus confirm our theoretical claims. On real-world cortical thickness data, our approach attains the accuracy of established discretizations, while conditioning on fewer than a tenth of the observations and providing a credible interval at every vertex.

title: Learning Without Clocks: Partition-Invariant Neural Network
summary: Event cameras, spiking cochleas and similar sensors emit asynchronous events, yet most learning systems first bin them into frames or packets, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced. Networks whose state is updated exactly at every event and evolves in closed form between events are invariant to this slicing. We ask what more makes the output (i) independent of the processing order of simultaneous events and (ii) continuous in the time stamps, even when two events cross in time, while (iii) staying sensitive to temporal order. For arbitrary nonlinear event models we prove that (i) and (ii) are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of the event updates, and that once updates commute, all order dependence comes from their non-commutation with the inter-event dynamics and vanishes linearly in the time lag. This identifies a class of time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models and yields a resolution-robustness bound for any model. We construct the minimal TM layer, a learnable, provably Lipschitz generalization of the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator; prove that no single additive layer can uniformly represent ordered pair interactions, whereas a three-dimensional TM state can; show that each TM layer adds two levels of temporal nesting versus one for additive layers; and give a single-layer higher-order construction (TM-k) and a stacking rule preserving all three properties. We instantiate these results as the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer, linear in the number of events, give a topology-free variant for temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods, and specify a preregistered clock-robustness protocol with a physical-time threat model for spike-retiming attacks. In preliminary development-set experiments, the TM state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5-9.1 points on DVS128 Gesture and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on SHD and Speech Commands.

title: On the Performance of AoA-Based Physical-Layer Authentication Under Multi-Source Impersonation Attacks
summary: This paper investigates cooperative impersonation attacks against angle-of-arrival (AoA)-based authentication for a wireless communication receiver equipped with a digital uniform linear array. Specifically, we characterize the vulnerability and robustness of this authentication system in relation to adversarial angular diversity and the relative numbers of adversarial sources and receive antennas. To this end, we first derive the optimal precoding vector for multiple spatially distributed adversarial sources by minimizing the mean squared error between legitimate and adversarial received signals. By means of the rank property of Vandermonde matrices, we then establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which the adversarial sources can reproduce the legitimate transmitter's spatial signature. With fewer adversarial sources than receive antennas, perfect reproduction is not possible without at least one adversarial source satisfying a specific AoA condition. In the other case, increasing the number of receive antennas can reduce impersonation success probabilities when none of the adversarial sources has an AoA satisfying this condition. Numerical results validate the theoretical analysis and evaluate the security performance of AoA-based authentication.

title: Outcome-dependent density combination by mixture Bayesian predictive synthesis
summary: In the problem of density combination, the decision maker receives multiple density functions and is tasked to learn which density is used most in which region of the outcome space, and to combine them into a single density. The outcome-dependent density combination can be cast as the Bayesian predictive synthesis, where the decision maker's uncertainty is naturally integrated. The models for the outcome-dependent weights have been considered in Johnson and West (2025), but limited to the Gaussian density kernel. In this study, we point out the limitation of the model flexibility of the Gaussian weights, and theoretically and numerically verify that the estimated weights can be least outcome-dependent. As an alternative, we propose the use of the softmax (logistic-normal) functions as the models for the weights, together with the bias-adjustment to the submitted densities. The posterior computation is feasible by using the custom Metropolis-Hastings method with the Pólya-gamma augmentation. The utility of the proposed method is illustrated in the real data analysis of movie theatre revenues, where a human expert reports the point quantile forecasts without any uncertainty quantification.

title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

title: Beyond Diagonal RIS for Physical-Layer Security: Low-Complexity Solution in the Low-SNR Regime
comment: Submitted for publication in IEEE journals
summary: This letter investigates beyond diagonal reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (BD-RIS) for physical-layer security (PLS) in correlated wiretap channels. A multi-antenna transmitter is considered, and transmit antenna selection (TAS) is used to exploit transmit-side diversity with a single active radio-frequency (RF) chain. Using the first-order secrecy rate approximation, we develop a two-stage scheme to maximize the secrecy rate in the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime. In the first stage, two TAS schemes are developed based on the effective channel upper-bound. In the second stage, an eigenvector-based BD-RIS scattering matrix is designed for single-connected, group-connected, and fully-connected architectures. Unlike legitimate-user-centric or eavesdropping-nulling designs, the proposed approach balances legitimate-user signal enhancement and information-leakage suppression without forcing zero leakage. Simulation results show improved secrecy performance, particularly under a strong correlation between legitimate and eavesdropping channels.

title: Sequince: a modular sequential Monte Carlo toolkit
comment: 7 pages. Describes sequince v0.1.0, available on PyPI. Code: https://github.com/sequince-dev/sequince. Documentation: https://sequince.readthedocs.io/. PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/sequince/
summary: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate sequences of probability distributions using populations of weighted samples and are widely applicable, including in Bayesian inference and particle filtering. We present sequince, a modular Python toolkit for constructing SMC algorithms from reusable and extensible components. The toolkit provides modular steps for weighting, resampling, mutation, transformation, and control operations that are composed to implement different algorithms. It also includes prebuilt samplers for tempered SMC, persistent sampling and nested sampling via SMC. Its core components follow the Python Array API standard, supporting NumPy, JAX, PyTorch, and CuPy, enabling analyses on CPUs or GPUs. Random-number control and checkpointing support reproducible scientific workflows. This paper describes sequince v0.1.0 and its design as reusable infrastructure for methodological research and application of SMC methods.

title: Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries
comment: 31 pages, full version of paper at NeurIPS 2026
summary: An AI developer often has several candidate versions of a system and can deploy a mixture of them, sending each request to a randomly chosen version, as in A/B testing. Each stakeholder (e.g., a safety team, a regulator, or a customer with private test data) accepts a mixture exactly when its expected performance (e.g., its rate of harmful replies) meets the stakeholder's own standard, which the developer can learn only by asking whether a proposed mixture is acceptable. We model this as choosing a lottery over $m$ alternatives for $n$ agents, each of whom accepts exactly the lotteries in an unknown halfspace and answers such binary membership queries. While Choo et al. (ICML 2026) sought a lottery that every agent accepts, none may exist when, say, safety and helpfulness requirements conflict, so we minimize the number of rejecting agents. We show that this problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and all utilities are $0$ or $1$.
