We then give exact algorithms that run in polynomial time when $m$ is constant, and in quasi-polynomial time when, for a constant $η$, some optimal lottery has no accepting agent within $η$ of its threshold. When only some agents can be queried, optimizing over a uniform sample of agents gives additive and relative guarantees for the whole population, with a sample size that does not depend on $n$, and a linear program gives a polynomial-time method for any $m$. On the other hand, for $m\ge 3$, a deterministic algorithm that queries only $K$ distinct agents cannot guarantee fewer than $n-K$ extra rejections, and this is achievable; in other words, it can guarantee nothing for the agents it does not ask. Small synthetic experiments indicate that our worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.

title: Non-Asymptotic Confidence Regions for Separable Nonlinear Models
comment: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)
summary: This paper studies robust uncertainty quantification for separable nonlinear least squares (SNLLS) problems. We propose two identification methods, (i) Residual-Perturbed Gradient (RPG) and (ii) Global-Fit-Gap (GFG), to construct joint distribution-free confidence regions for both the linear and nonlinear parameters. By exploiting assumed group invariance of the noise (such as symmetry or exchangeability), we apply random perturbations (such as sign-changes or permutations) to build the regions based on resampling and ranking. We prove that both methods guarantee non-asymptotically exact coverage (type I error). Finally, we illustrate the constructions through two numerical experiments: (i) identifying generalized finite impulse response (GFIR) systems using Laguerre polynomials with an adjustable decay rate and (ii) fitting Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) models with variable knots and widths.

title: Adaptive Sequential Surveillance of Infectious Diseases Under Limited Sampling Capacity
comment: The abstract of this project has been accepted for poster presentation at the Royal Statistical Society 2026 International Conference
summary: This paper develops a closed-loop adaptive sequential surveillance framework for infectious disease monitoring with limited surveillance resources. In this framework, we use a Bayesian spatio-temporal model to predict disease prevalence at each location, and propose several adaptive site-allocation strategies based on the posterior probabilities that the predictions exceed a predefined threshold. These strategies exploit high-risk locations while also exploring, by random or recency-based sampling or by incorporating the frontiers of emerging outbreaks. To address the unequal inclusion probabilities induced by adaptive sampling, we integrate inverse-probability weighting (IPW) into each model update. A simulation study showed that adaptive surveillance strategies improved outbreak detection relative to uniform sampling and fixed sentinel sampling. Frontier-based strategies improved detection and timeliness relative to risk-proportional allocation. When IPW was used to update the model, some proposed strategies yielded lower inferential bias compared with the standard unweighted update, particularly for strategies that allowed more flexible exploration. Credible-interval coverage varied by strategy. The results identify trade-offs between exploitation of known high-risk locations and exploration of potential outbreak frontiers.

title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
comment: ACM TheWebConf2027 8 pages main content 4 pages appendix
summary:
AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost.
  We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines.
  We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

title: Conformal Prediction-Aware DOA Tracking
comment: Presented at the 2026 Israeli Conference on Systems and Electrical Engineering (ICSEE 2026)
summary: We introduce an uncertainty-aware DOA-tracking framework combining deep posterior estimation, conformal-prediction calibration, and temporal smoothing. The approach enhances stability against reverberation and burst-like directional noise, yielding more reliable trajectories and greater robustness than conventional DOA-tracking methods.

title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

title: Depth through Recurrence: Towards Ultra-Efficient On-Device ASR
summary: Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved remarkable accuracy by scaling model depth and capacity, but at the cost of increased memory, energy, and computational demands. On edge devices where ASR is often most needed, such as watches and glasses, deploying such large models is infeasible due to extremely constrained resources. This raises a fundamental question: can we achieve high representational power in deep ASR models without scaling up parameterization? In this work, we revisit the role of depth and identify layer wise representational dynamics, in which most layers learn functionally similar transformations. Motivated by this insight, we propose a block-recurrent ASR architecture that replaces parameterized depth with a small set of recurrent blocks, each consisting of weight-shared layers, thereby preserving effective depth while drastically reducing model size. Through representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation, block-recurrent models retain the accuracy of large reference models while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks, a model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of the accuracy of large models on average. The compact backbone further enables efficient on-device personalization through lightweight MoE-LoRA adaptation, allowing user-specific models to match or surpass the accuracy of general-purpose ASR systems with significantly lower inference cost. By reusing weights across recurrent steps, the proposed architecture reduces memory-access overhead and inference energy consumption. Together, these results show that high quality ASR can be achieved without large parameterization, and that structured recurrence provides a principled path towards ultra-compressed, energy-efficient, and personalized speech recognition on the edge.

title: Human Activity Recognition using Ceiling-Mounted Multi-Radar Sensors
summary: Continuous activity monitoring in assisted living should work without cameras or wearable devices. Radar meets this requirement, but most radar studies use a single sensor and activities recorded in isolation, and few deliver results in real time. We present an indoor monitoring system in which point clouds from three ceiling-mounted radar sensors are fused using density-based clustering, movement and posture features are derived for activity classification, and results are shown on a real-time dashboard. In a preliminary study with eight participants performing everyday activities as one continuous scenario, a random forest reached 74% frame-level accuracy with a random 80/20 split and 68% with leave-one-participant-out evaluation. Without position features, accuracy fell to 46% and 44%, indicating partial dependence on room layout, while window-level features without position reached 67% and 65%.

title: Graphical Modeling from Marginal Information via Optimal Transport
summary: A graphical model represents multivariate interactions through conditional independence, but requires jointly observed samples to be fitted to data. When individuals cannot be tracked and only marginal observations are available, as with destructive measurements leading to cross-sectional data, the problem of graphical modeling is confounded with that of assembling a joint law. We show how simultaneous graphical modeling and joint law assembly can be realized via a multi-marginal optimal transport problem with graphical cost. Focusing on Gaussian marginals, we generate a joint law satisfying the Markov properties prescribed by a given graph. Within the class of joint distributions respecting the graph and marginals constraints, our construction selects a member by making the interactions set by the graph as strong as possible under a dependence budget measured by relative entropy. In the empirical setting, where only estimates of the marginals are available, we examine the stability of the problem under perturbations of both the marginals and of the graph weights. The resulting error splits into an estimation term, vanishing with the sample size, and a specification term, which quantifies the cost of a misspecified graph. Finally, we illustrate these findings by numerical experiments.

title: TensorBound: Characterizing Tensor Binding Failures in AI Compiler and Runtime Stacks
summary: AI compiler and runtime stacks must preserve bindings between tensor values and their operations, storage, and execution state. These bindings can fail while the underlying objects remain present, with symptoms appearing in another layer. We present TensorBound, an empirical study of tensor binding failures in IREE and the XLA and PyTorch ecosystems. The study analyzes 264 reports and reconstructs 149 distinct repaired causes through source tracing and comparisons of pre-fix and repaired revisions. Each reconstruction connects the first invalid decision to its violated condition, physical effect, and repair. Missing eligibility checks, incorrect mappings or translations, and lost or omitted relations account for 69.1% of repaired causes. These patterns highlight the need to preserve binding facts and check the conditions for their use. The 101 first invalid decisions in compiler code identify candidate checking points before execution. Four archived IREE diagnostic attempts distinguish effect localization from source-based cause explanation. Together, these findings motivate transition-specific checks that preserve binding facts across representations and enforce the required conditions at consuming decisions.

title: Implementation and Validation of Mismatch-Tolerant High-Gain OTA with a Calibrated Negative Conductance Load
summary: This paper presents the circuit-level implementation of a mismatch-tolerant high-gain operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) using automatic negative-conductance calibration in 65-nm CMOS. The technique enhances OTA gain by compensating for its finite output conductance using a cross-coupled transistor pair, with an on-chip calibration loop that eliminates the need for a replica circuit or external tuning. The calibration routine increases the gain by driving the steady state error of the OTA in a unity gain feedback loop toward zero. The implementation addresses practical challenges involving comparator offset, DAC design, and subtractor gain and offset. A 6-bit capacitive DAC (CDAC)-based comparator offset calibration scheme enables reliable detection of the sub-millivolt steady state error required for high OTA gain. Post-layout Monte Carlo simulations show that the comparator offset standard deviation is reduced from 4.11 mV to 132 $μ$V, with a maximum observed post-calibration offset of 625 $μ$V. The complete calibration circuitry is implemented and evaluated through post-layout simulations.

title: Graphical Models Induced by Irreversible Event Accumulation on Trees
summary:
Decomposable graphical models are usually adopted for their computational convenience rather than derived from a data-generating mechanism. We show that a special class of them arises naturally from the irreversible accumulation of events along a branching history. Each event is attached to an edge of a latent rooted tree and is inherited by everything below that edge; an observation records which events have occurred at a randomly chosen node, not necessarily a leaf. When the tree is a path, this is the cumulative coding of an ordinal variable, whose indicators form a Markov chain; in the general tree case the Markov chain is replaced by a junction tree.
  The conditional independence graph of the event indicators is always decomposable and, in fact, is the line graph of the tree (maximal cliques correspond to nodes where two or more edges meet and separators are the single events on the edges joining two such nodes). The graph determines the tree up to the choice of root. A connected graph arises in this way if, and only if, it is chordal, any two of its maximal cliques share at most one vertex, no vertex is in three maximal cliques, and the graph is such that any two maximal cliques share at most one vertex. This provides a simple graphical test for compatibility with the mechanism (necessary but not sufficient, as irreversibility also constrains the distribution's support).
  The structure breaks down if we look at just the leaves, and measurement error destroys the exact screening and leads to a denser graph rather than simply a weaker dependence. We discuss inference, provide diagnostics for departures such as recurrent events, illustrate them on some simulated data and discuss their application in the context of mutation accumulation and lineage tracing where both ancestral and descendant types are sampled together.

title: Improving Data-Constrained Scaling with Hyperparameter Transfer and Ensembling
summary: As growing compute budgets outpace the growth of high-quality training data, large language models must be trained with both compute and data constraints in mind. Unfortunately, existing prescriptions for data-constrained scaling suffer from two important limitations. First, past works hold key hyperparameters such as weight decay fixed with scale, despite the fact that optimal hyperparameters vary wildly with model size and number of epochs. Second, past works neglect ensembling, a promising axis for scaling under data constraints. As a surprising consequence, prior prescriptions can lead to loss that increases with compute budget. We address both limitations by fitting power laws that prescribe how to transfer hyperparameters with scale and scaling laws that prescribe how to allocate compute with ensembling. Training on 100M tokens from FineWeb, our recipe reduces validation loss by over 0.15 nats compared to prior recipes, a 14% decrease in perplexity, and achieves monotonic improvements with compute through ensembling. These gains are achieved using prescriptions fit to smaller runs and validated at up to 12$\times$ larger compute budgets.

title: Computing with Coupled Oscillator Networks: Optimization, Memory, and Modern AI Primitives
summary: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.

title: Fisher Contrastive Learning to Mitigate Feature Suppression: A Case Study in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia Diagnosis
comment: 31 pages, including supplementary material; 3 figures and 2 tables
summary: Self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) learns representations by contrasting augmented views of the same sample, but it can exhibit feature suppression, where dominant or easy-to-learn factors suppress other class-relevant signals, degrading the performance of representations, particularly in high-dimensional data with heterogeneous features. We introduce Fisher Contrastive Learning (FCL), which uses a regularized Fisher trace criterion to address feature suppression. FCL learns embeddings by maximizing the discriminative strength of Fisher discriminant functions, producing representations that preserve class-relevant information implied by the augmentation process. We prove that the representations learned by FCL could alleviate the feature suppression effects. We demonstrate FCL on simulated benchmarks designed to induce feature suppression and on a real-world biomedical application, pretraining on large white blood cell microscopy image dataset and transfer learning for diagnosis of acute promyelocytic leukemia in an external cohort. In all experiments, FCL outperforms the self-supervised baselines and yields more robust and discriminative representations.

title: Convex Potential Learning for Optimal Transport Between Medical Images
summary: Computing optimal transport maps between medical images plays a fundamental role in morphological analysis. However, existing methods are either difficult to scale to large 3D medical images or rely on regularized formulations that provide only approximate transport maps. To improve the accuracy of downstream medical image analysis, we propose a novel approach for estimating optimal transport maps by parameterizing the convex potential function. By construction, the resulting transport map is guaranteed to be curl-free, consistent with Brenier's theorem. We evaluate the proposed method on both 2D and 3D medical imaging datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves lower transport estimation errors and produces higher-quality image reconstructions than existing methods.

title: The Importance of Speech Genre for End-of-Turn Detector Training
summary: End-of-turn (EoT) detection has been studied mostly through features, models, and modalities, while the speech genre of the training data has drawn far less attention. We isolate this factor. Using one reproducible annotation pipeline, we build a matched pair of corpora, multi-turn human-human conversational and single-turn human-machine, and train the same streaming ConvLSTM EoT detector on each. Across four test sets the conversational model reaches up to +0.45 higher F1, driven by fewer false alarms on the mid-turn pauses and hesitations that are rare in single-turn corpora. This conversational-training effect is not specific to frame-level decoding. Under a matched complete-or-not test it also appears at the utterance level, across two encoders, but only on conversational test data. Testing only on single-turn speech, as most prior work does, therefore hides the benefit of conversational training data. Against open-source baselines, our 1.8M-parameter model attains the highest F1 on every test set.

title: Model-assisted estimation of the finite population mean via local linear regression with associated kernels
summary: In this paper, we propose a general regression-assisted estimator of the population mean based on local regression with associated kernels, a broad class that encompasses both classical (symmetric) kernels, such as the Gaussian and Epanechnikov kernels, and asymmetric kernels, such as the gamma kernel. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator, including explicit expressions for the bias, mean squared error, and asymptotic normality, under a unified framework that applies to any kernel in this class. Through simulation studies on nonnegative data and one real-data application, we compare the finite-sample performance of the estimator based on the gamma kernel with those relying on the Gaussian and Epanechnikov kernels. When the data are supported on the positive real line, symmetric kernels suffer from boundary bias near zero due to mass assignment outside the support, whereas the gamma kernel, naturally adapted to $[0,\infty)$, alleviates this effect. The results confirm that the choice of kernel within the associated matters in practice, and that asymmetric kernels provide a reliable and efficient alternative when the underlying regression function is supported on the positive real line or exhibits marked asymmetry.

title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
summary: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept, and it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts. In a simulated market with five conditions (no collusion, a joint reward with neutral messages, the same with an openly stated intention, a covert first-letter code, and the code with a stated intention), PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one reading the speaker's messages answered "no" in all 50 markets, and one reading every seller's messages flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion. PoPLi detects the use of a private channel, not collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.

title: Towards Multilingual End-of-Turn Detection using Frozen Speech Encoders
summary: A spoken dialogue system must judge when the user has yielded the floor. This end-of-turn (EoT) detector is normally trained and tuned afresh for each language, which is costly to scale to new languages. We instead build one on a frozen multilingual encoder, training only a small fixed-size head. Using five CALLHOME languages, we investigate three questions. First, how well a head trained on one language transfers zero-shot to the others. Second, how much target-language adaptation is required to recover full task performance. Third, whether a single fixed decision threshold holds across languages without per-language tuning. We find that the head transfers well, even between tonal and pitch-accent languages, and that a few hours of audio recover nearly all the loss, matching in-language training. A frozen multilingual encoder with one lightweight head is a practical, language-agnostic baseline for EoT detection.

title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
summary: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $χ^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.

title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
summary: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.

title: Neuromorphic design of a rhythmic network
comment: This is an author-created, un-copyedited version of an article submitted for publication in the Journal of Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering. IOP Publishing Ltd is not responsible for any errors or omissions in this version of the manuscript or any version derived from it
summary: Central Pattern Generators (CPGs) have long inspired the design of rhythms that combine endogenous generation and exogenous interaction. In neurodynamics and engineering studies, CPGs have been primarily analysed and designed as networks of coupled oscillators. In contrast, the present article regards CPGs as networks that propagate events through excitable rather than oscillatory nodes. The proposed event-based perspective reduces the design of network-level rhythmic properties to the tuning of local nodal input-output characteristics. This reduction enables a distributed and robust design methodology: nodes can be tuned independently, they can be heterogeneous, and the global rhythm results from local event propagation rather than from a specific global tuning of the network parameters. The present article builds on previously introduced concepts that parallel existing characterizations of oscillators: the event describing function (eDF), which characterises the propagation delay of a node, and the event phase response curve (ePRC), which characterises the phase sensitivity of a node. Event-based CPGs made of excitable rather than oscillatory nodes emerge as a principled design framework for robust rhythm generation.

title: Hidden Disparities in Ranking: Category-Aware Fairness via Distributional Stability
summary: We study the problem of fair ranking in recommender systems. We provide a formal probabilistic framework in which ranking policies are distributions over permutations, and the utility of a user is the exposure given to the items they interact with, relative to that of an ideal ranking. We consider utility parity across user groups, as well as its category-aware refinement, conditional utility parity, which requires parity within each category of items. Following a recent view of fairness as distributional stability, we show that both criteria are equivalent to the stability of the utility under changes in the composition of user groups. Optimizing over mixtures of ranking policies leads to a second-order cone program, for which we provide generalization bounds. A numerical study validates our theoretical findings.

title: Modeling and Parametrization of Large-scale Hydrogen Electrolyzers for Transient and Frequency Stability Analysis
summary: Hydrogen Electrolyzers (HEs), particularly Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM)-based systems, are flexible loads capable of providing grid ancillary services and enhancing the stability of renewable-dominated power systems due to their fast electrical response. However, the literature often lacks clear guidance on the structure, modeling, and parametrization of large-scale HEs for transient and frequency stability analyses. This paper presents a detailed configuration for utility-scale HE plants, using the stack as the fundamental unit, supported by a realistic parametrization based on commercial components. Furthermore, this work extends the Generalized ESS Model (GEM), a linearized state-space model previously utilized with other converter-interfaced energy storage systems, to PEM HEs for the first time. To facilitate plant scalability, a robust method for scaling GEM matrices across different capacities is proposed. Finally, a measurement-based methodology is developed to estimate the GEM parameters and subsequently extract the equivalent electrical circuit parameters. Comprehensive simulations on the WSCC system under various disturbances validate the accuracy of the derived GEM, the effectiveness of the scaling approach, and the robustness of the parameter identification methodology.

title: Understanding axial attention in TSFMs through single location regression
summary: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.

title: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback
summary: Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts. We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within K sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models' iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.

title: SpeakerTurn: Target-Speaker Semantic Turn Detection in Multi-Speaker Environments
summary: Semantic completeness alone cannot determine when an assistant should respond in a multi-speaker environment: a completed utterance may belong to an interfering speaker, while the designated user is still speaking, acknowledging, or requesting time. We therefore study semantic turn inference conditioned on speaker identity. We propose SpeakerTurn, a framework that jointly predicts the target transcript and turn state from a speech mixture and an independent target-speaker reference. Built on CocktailASR-1, it links semantic decisions to the corresponding target content through joint supervision, distinguishing complete, incomplete, backchannel, wait, and target-absent states, with a separate interruption task. We also examine whether structured chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision improves decisions by representing speaker presence and semantic cues. On a synthetic multi-speaker test set, SpeakerTurn achieves five-state macro F1 of 0.811 and target-transcription character error rate (CER) of 4.20%, correctly resolving all ten reference-swapped interruption pairs. Joint-format transcription and native-interface recognition nevertheless behave differently, and CoT improves validation transcription without improving turn macro F1. These results show why target attribution, semantic turn discrimination, and recognition retention require separate assessment when adapting speech language models for speaker-conditioned interaction.

title: Homogeneity Pursuit of Panel Data with Sparsity
summary: In panel data analysis, studying individual attributes is important for both methodological development and practical applications. Homogeneity in individual attributes and sparsity in coefficients are therefore important topics, as they help uncover relationships among individuals and identify the truly relevant covariates. However, many existing approaches do not explicitly exploit the potential grouping information contained in separately fitted individual-level penalized estimators to identify latent groups. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical group recovery approach based on sparse initial estimation to jointly identify latent groups and sparse parameter structures in panel data. We first introduce a basic version that can efficiently identify homogeneity and sparsity. Based on this basic version, we further introduce a local search step to improve the performance of our method. Compared with existing methods, our approach shows the best overall performance when jointly considering estimation accuracy and computational efficiency. The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of our approach over existing approaches. We further apply the proposed approach to a real dataset to show its practical applicability.

title: Effects of Deep Learning Architecture and Pretraining on Automated Vocal Fold Segmentation in Ex Vivo High-Speed Phonation Images
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) intraglottal particle image velocimetry (PIV) of ex vivo phonation experiments quantifies vocal fold medial surface dynamics and the intraglottal flow field. However, it relies on manual segmentation because residual glare, low tissue-to-flow contrast, and tracer-particle speckle obscure the vocal fold boundaries. This study assessed how deep learning architecture and ImageNet pretraining affect automated vocal fold segmentation in these high-speed images. Four established architectures from three categories were benchmarked: the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based UNet and UNet++, the hybrid CNN-transformer-based TransUNet, and the pure transformer-based Swin-UNet, the latter two trained from scratch and from ImageNet-pretrained weights. Using 16,344 expert-annotated images from 227 phonation trials of excised canine larynges, the six pipelines were trained with five seeds under a standardized protocol and compared on 50 held-out test trials using trial-level Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) spanned only 0.9734 to 0.9764, so the pipelines differed mainly in boundary fidelity. Pretraining significantly improved the boundary F1 score (BF1) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of the TransUNet and Swin-UNet, about four times more for the Swin-UNet. Once pretrained, the two performed similarly, although the Swin-UNet has only about a quarter of the trainable parameters. Without pretraining, the TransUNet had a significantly higher BF1 and a lower HD95 than both CNN-based pipelines and about half their share of images with HD95 > 50 pixels. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply deep learning to vocal fold segmentation in 2D intraglottal PIV, and it offers a reference framework for segmenting experimental flow-visualization images with noisy optical conditions or highly deformable objects.

title: Which wind and solar modelling choices matter? Effects on capacity factors, energy droughts and European power system configuration
summary: Europe's future power system will rely heavily on wind and solar power and must remain resilient during prolonged periods of low wind and solar generation, known as variable renewable energy (VRE) droughts. To capture such rare events, adequacy assessments increasingly draw on decades of weather data, but the conversion of weather into power is largely treated as fixed. It remains unclear which modelling choices in this conversion matter for representing these droughts, and whether they matter as much as the weather itself. Here we systematically compare these choices side by side (bias correction, wind speed extrapolation, capacity layouts, turbine and photovoltaic configurations, and wake losses) and trace their effects through VRE droughts to the design of a net-zero European power system, using 85 years of reanalysis data. We find that modelling choices barely change how often VRE droughts occur or when the system is stressed. They do, however, determine how much capacity is needed to withstand that stress. By altering the electricity delivered during droughts, they shift required capacity by up to 480 GW, which is comparable to the spread across the most critical weather years. Modelling exercises should therefore use multiple weather years; bias-correct and regionally validate weather inputs; explicitly represent resource heterogeneity, forward-looking technologies, and wake losses; and judge these choices by their effect on the low-generation tail, not only on the mean.

title: Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert Review: Application to Online Cell-Type Labeling
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models can accelerate cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but safely scaling their use requires determining, with error control, which model-generated labels can be accepted without expert review. This is challenging in evolving workflows because cell morphology and type composition may change across tissue regions and slides, making one-time calibration unreliable. We propose Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift (CARED), a distribution-free framework that leverages randomized expert audit to achieve long-run error control for AI-assisted annotation under distribution shift. For each incoming batch, CARED uniformly selects a subset of cases for expert review and uses the acquired labels to calibrate later decisions. Among unreviewed cases, CARED determines a subset of them to safely skip expert labeling, while suggesting candidate labels for the others for downstream resolution. We prove that this workflow provides long-run control of cumulative error over both the full stream and the cells outside of the audit sample, without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions. We further enhance the framework by introducing class-conditional guarantees to ensure error control within important but rare cell types, together with a utility module to target more automatic resolutions, smaller candidate sets, and greater biological coherence, without compromising validity. Experiments on pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams, together with a stream constructed from real expert annotations, show that CARED controls the cumulative errors while a substantial fraction of cells (up to 70%) bypass expert review.

title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
summary: As AI systems increasingly mediate human communication, identifying conditions under which they augment collective sense-making is a critical challenge. Through a randomized experiment (N=1,173 U.S. participants across 391 small-group deliberations), we investigate whether AI-guided self-reflection improves subsequent deliberative discourse. We show that engaging with a non-directive AI chatbot instructed to structure self-reflection prior to group deliberation yields significantly higher deliberation quality (measured by the Discourse Quality Index, DQI) compared to a baseline of no self-reflection (Cohen's d=0.31) and a condition of unassisted self-reflection (d=0.27), and the positive impact is most pronounced in groups with disagreement. This improvement may be driven by more sophisticated argument justifications, greater consensus-building effort, and increased respect for counterarguments. Furthermore, after self-reflection, participants in the AI condition reported higher empathy toward dissenting peers and a deeper understanding of opposing reasoning. Beyond observed behavior, our findings are empirically relevant to open debates between political philosophy and psychology surrounding self-reflection, demonstrating that interactive AI could transform solitary thinking into productive internal reflection. Together, these results demonstrate that even simple AI-based reflective scaffolds can foster more productive group dynamics, opening new avenues for leveraging AI to augment collective intelligence.

title: AKDQ: Adaptive Key-Delta Quantization for Low-Bitrate RVQ-based Neural Speech Codecs
summary: Low-bitrate speech coding is essential for bandwidth-constrained channels and on-device applications, but conventional residual vector quantization (RVQ)-based codecs employ a fixed number of codebooks per frame regardless of content. Adjacent speech frames often exhibit strong similarity, and quantizing them independently with the same scheme results in redundant encoding, thereby wasting bitrate. Therefore, we propose Adaptive Key-Delta Quantization (AKDQ), which replaces the fixed per-frame VQ allocation of RVQ with an adaptive frame-wise key-or-delta policy. AKDQ is a plug-in strategy that requires no modification to the codec's encoder-decoder backbone. Specifically, in AKDQ, each frame is classified as either a key-frame (K-frame) quantized with all VQs, or a delta-frame (D-frame) quantized with only a few VQs on a delta correction from the previous reconstruction, thereby reducing bitrate. The K/D decision is made by a budget-aware causal scheduler through a bit-bank mechanism, keeping the system streamable with no additional lookahead. Experiments on both causal and non-causal codec families demonstrate that AKDQ effectively reduces bitrate redundancy. For instance, on DAC, using AKDQ at 1.5 kbps achieves reconstruction quality comparable to using the baseline RVQ at 2.0 kbps, saving 25% of the bitrate.

title: Statistical Analysis of Synthetic Data with Verification: A Linear Regression Framework
summary: Synthetic data are widely used for training modern AI systems. However, their statistical understanding remains limited. It is well recognized in statistics that repeated self-training on synthetic data can amplify errors inherited from pre-trained models, leading to model collapse. Verification plays a crucial role in selecting high-quality synthetic data to help prevent model collapse and improve model performance. We study verified self-training in a linear regression framework, where a pre-trained estimator generates synthetic data with injected generation noise and a verifier selects samples according to a verification threshold. Post-training on the accepted samples updates either all coordinates (full fine-tuning) or only an active subset (partial fine-tuning). Our analysis reveals three potentially counterintuitive effects. We establish that tighter verification does not always lead to lower prediction risk. We also find that a suitable level of injected generation noise can reduce prediction risk, while excessive noise can increase it. Moreover, full and partial fine-tuning can respond differently to the same verification rule, since pre-training error in the frozen coordinates affects both sample selection and post-training risk. We analyze these effects by deriving finite sample risk bounds for four separate regimes determined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error. The bounds precisely characterize how verification affects prediction risk across these regimes. In particular, we quantify how the generation noise, the effective accepted sample size, and the covariance of the accepted covariates affect prediction risk. The analysis extends to iterative verified full fine-tuning, where sufficiently tight verification reduces the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.

title: DropFENO: A Data-Free, Physics-Based Operator-Learning Framework for Droplet Equilibria on Mixed-Wettability Patterned Surfaces
summary: We study whether the equilibrium of a drop on a chemically patterned wall, and the capillary forces that the pattern exerts on it, can be learned from the free energy alone, without solution data. We introduce DropFENO (Droplet Free-Energy Neural Operator), in which Fourier (FNO), tensor-factorised Fourier (TFNO) and wavelet (WNO) neural operators are trained in two and three dimensions on the diffuse-interface free energy of the drop, with its volume and centroid constraints imposed as penalties. The predictions are tested with the virtual-work (Hellmann--Feynman) theorem: the force exerted by the pattern on a held drop is a wall integral of the equilibrium field which, for a drop straddling a wettability step, reduces identically to the contact-line law $F=σΔ\cosθ\,L$. DropFENO reproduces this law and the energy landscape of a drop crossing a step, and reproduces the pinning of the receding contact line less accurately. The residual error lies in the soft modes of the capillary energy (small displacements of the interface and the contact line). This explains why the energy is predicted accurately while contact-line positions are not, and why on striped walls the operators return Cassie-like states instead of the edge-pinned states whose anisotropic apparent angles the reference minimiser shares with lattice Boltzmann simulations. On held-out patterned walls the median energy of the predictions lies $\NdEmedRandFnoTwo$ of the free-drop energy above the best known minimum (FNO, two dimensions), at about one hundredth of the cost of a per-instance minimisation, and a refinement by a classical solver started from the prediction returns the reference state in almost all cases.

title: Integrated Sensing and Communication via Channel Knowledge Maps Built from Beam Feedback Coefficients
summary: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) support wireless localization by linking channel features to user locations. Detailed channel fingerprints, however, can require substantial storage. This paper proposes a CKM-based localization framework that uses beam feedback coefficients collected during communication. These coefficients serve as compact location fingerprints within the beam management process, without requiring full channel feedback or additional sensing measurements. Using a coarse position prior, the base station searches nearby CKM entries and refines the location estimate through local interpolation. We analyze the relationship between spatial fingerprint variation and localization accuracy, and evaluate the effect of feedback quantization. Simulations show favorable storage--accuracy trade-offs relative to dense and sparsified spectral fingerprinting in the tested multipath environments.

title: Reframing Spatial Uncertainty Visualisation with a Layered Grammar of Graphics
summary: Communicating both estimated values and their associated uncertainties presents a particular challenge in spatial visualisation because spatial coordinates already occupy the primary visual channels, leaving relatively few channels available for encoding uncertainty alongside the estimated values. A range of visualisation techniques has been developed to address this challenge, including bivariate choropleth maps, pixel maps, and glyph maps. However, existing implementations typically treat these techniques as dedicated visualisations rather than expressing them through the composable elements of a grammar of graphics. We reframe uncertainty visualisation as an extension of the layered grammar of graphics, allowing uncertainty-specific representations to be composed, customised, and extended alongside other graphical components. We demonstrate this perspective by integrating uncertainty visualisation into the layered architecture of ggplot2, accommodating these techniques while also motivating new approaches such as the dual map for selective attention between estimated values and their associated uncertainties. We implement the framework in the R package ggincerta and demonstrate its application through three case studies.

title: Echo: Scaling Visual Reinforcement Learning with Off-policy Experience
summary: Scaling visual reinforcement learning (RL) with GPU-accelerated simulation is computationally expensive due to rendering and visual-policy inference costs. Consequently, two-stage teacher--student distillation is commonly used to train visual policies, but introduces an imitation gap. In this preliminary study, we introduce \echomethod{}, \textbf{a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales experience collection without proportionally increasing visual computation}. Through \textbf{inverse distillation}, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects inexpensive, unrendered experience. Echo leverages this experience for off-policy value learning, directly improving the visual policy through a shared privileged critic. We instantiate \echomethod{} with FastTD3 and evaluate it on three visual control tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis. Relative to \sdpgmethod{} under the evaluated configurations, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of \textbf{60\% across the three locomotion tasks} and \textbf{56\% across both hand tasks}, while improving peak mean returns by \textbf{62\% and 12\%}, respectively. Both hand tasks also achieve higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets. These initial results suggest that scaling off-policy experience is a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL.

title: LC-Resonance Placement Limits and Damping Recovery in Virtual-Admittance-Based Grid-Forming Inverter Control
summary: Compact LC-filter design and inner-loop control must be coordinated for stable grid-forming operation. This paper quantifies how current-loop proportional gain constrains LC-resonance placement in virtual-admittance-based dual-loop control with unity voltage-feedback decoupling (VFD) and capacitor-voltage active damping. Equivalent-impedance analysis identifies gain-dependent contraction of the positive-resistance region. Delayed inverter-current feedback opposes VFD-assisted damping above one-sixth of the sampling frequency. Simple proportional-path frequency shaping recovers an admissible effective-gain window while retaining unity VFD and leaving the resonant path unchanged. Reduced-model criteria, checked against the complete model, link window closure to a nominal resonance-placement limit near one-third of the sampling frequency under single-sampled single-update operation over the studied gain range. A 3-kVA prototype demonstrates an 83.3% LC-product reduction at comparable voltage and nominal current crossovers. A separate comparison with the same high-resonance filter demonstrates stable operation at 2.68 times the unshaped nominal current crossover. Output-impedance analysis and grid-connected tests identify additional grid-dependent gain constraints.

title: Enhanced convergence guarantees of score-based generative models in $\mathcal{W}_2$-distance beyond log-concavity
summary: Although score-based generative models (SGMs) have achieved remarkable success in real-world sample generation tasks, it is still far from sufficient to understand them from a mathematical perspective. In this paper, we aim to provide enhanced convergence guarantees for two existing SGMs in $\mathcal{W}_2$-distance beyond log-concavity. More precisely, we develop a novel framework of {\color{black}discretization} error analysis for Euler-Maruyama (EM) and Poisson midpoint (PM) time discretization schemes for SGMs. Under a non-log-concavity condition, we show that $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d}/ε)$ iterations suffice to approximate the target distributions in $ε$-accuracy for the classical EM-based SGM, considerably improving upon the existing iteration complexity $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d/ε^2)$. Notably, the novel framework of error analysis also enables us to establish an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d}/ε^{2/3})$ iteration complexity for the PM-based SGM in $ε$-accuracy, significantly outperforming current state-of-the-art Wasserstein convergence guarantees for SDE-based diffusion samplers.

title: What Constitutes Food Similarity? Visual Representations and Retrieval in Indian Cuisine
summary: Food similarity underlies retrieval, recommendation, substitution, and other food computing tasks, yet food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation. We ask what happens to food similarity beyond identity: how different visual representations organize foods into relational neighborhoods, what culinary relationships these neighborhoods reveal or obscure, and how consistently these structures emerge across representations. Indian cuisine provides a challenging setting in which visually similar foods may have different culinary identities, while foods within a culinary family can vary substantially in appearance. Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations spanning convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, we evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examining culinary-family structure, contrast cases, and cross-representation agreement. We also aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. At the dish level, aggregation reveals common visual structure despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These findings show that recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure: food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection. Understanding these structures is therefore a prerequisite to combining multiple food information modalities into a coherent notion of similarity.

title: Safe Platooning under Input Constraints with Link-Wise Velocity String Stability
summary: We propose a decentralized controller for vehicle platoons with different braking and propulsion limits. The method uses only local distance and velocity measurements and requires neither online optimization nor exact vehicle parameters. The design combines a braking-distance safety margin with an adaptive funnel that relaxes the spacing requirement during propulsion saturation. A standstill mechanism prevents backward motion and supports stop-and-go operation. Under explicit uniform conditions on the vehicle parameters, controller settings, and initial states, we prove that closed-loop solutions exist for all time, collisions are avoided, and input limits are satisfied. Moreover, each follower tracks its predecessor's velocity range with gain one, up to an explicit additive offset determined by the funnel width and the braking-distance term. This bound establishes link-wise velocity string stability. Both the offset and the bounds on speeds and spacing errors are independent of vehicle index and platoon length. Simulations with 2 to 100 followers illustrate safety and bounded velocity deviations under disturbances and actuator limits.

title: Optimal Neural Estimation for High-Dimensional Nonparametric Regression under Multisource Covariate Shift
summary: We study high-dimensional nonparametric regression under multisource covariate shift, where $\mathrm J$ sources of training data share a common regression function but differ in their covariate distributions, sample sizes, and noise variances. Our goal is to combine these sources to estimate the regression function accurately under a target covariate distribution. We propose an oracle weighted neural estimator and establish its minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors through matching upper and lower bounds. The resulting rate is $\mathsf n_{\rm eff}^{-2p/(2p+K)}$, where $p$ and $K$ denote the effective smoothness and dimension of the regression function, and the effective sample size is \begin{align} \mathsf n_{\rm eff} =\sum_{j=1}^{\mathrm J} \frac{n_j}{(1+σ_{ρ,j})σ_{ε,j}^{2}}. \nonumber \end{align} Here, $n_j$ is the sample size of source $j$, $σ_{ε,j}^{2}$ is its noise variance, and $σ_{ρ,j}$ controls the deviation between the covariate distribution of source $j$ and the target covariate distribution. We also develop an adaptive procedure that requires no knowledge of source noise variances or covariate-shift parameters. Under suitable conditions, this procedure attains the oracle minimax rate up to logarithmic factors.

title: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as automated judges, yet most alignment methods target aggregated human judgments and overlook variation among individual annotators. Existing approaches to matching the full distribution of human ratings mainly rely on output-level calibration or parameter fine-tuning. We propose Human-Residual Steering (HRS), to our knowledge the first method to align frozen LLM judges with human judgment distributions through learned hidden-state interventions. An oracle analysis shows that low-rank corrections at a single layer remove most of the discrepancy between judge and human distributions. HRS learns to predict such corrections from the judge's hidden representation and rating logits, training on individual annotations with proper scoring rules for ordinal and nominal judgments and optimising through the frozen downstream layers. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, HRS outperforms all evaluated frozen-weight baselines. With Qwen2.5-7B, it achieves the lowest Jensen-Shannon distance on 13 of 14 benchmarks, reducing the mean from 0.565 to 0.352 versus 0.377 for the strongest calibrator. HRS also raises mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores from 0.449 to 0.579, improves population-level estimation under limited annotation budgets, and trains about 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest cost in alignment.

title: Blind Video Denoising for Vocal Tract rtMRI using a Self-Supervised Ensemble
summary: Real-time magnetic resonance imaging of the vocal tract makes speech articulation directly observable, but the trade-off between temporal resolution and signal quality introduces substantial noise and obscures fine articulatory detail. Since clean references cannot be acquired for a moving vocal tract, supervised denoising approaches are not applicable in this setting. We propose a self-supervised denoising framework that combines spatiotemporal super-resolution learning with pseudo-supervision derived from a variance-stabilized non-local means filter. A dual-model fusion strategy balances noise suppression and preservation of high-frequency articulatory structure. Experiments on the USC-75 multi-speaker dataset under natural noise conditions show that the ensemble raises the signal-to-noise ratio by 11.9 dB on unseen subjects while attaining more high-frequency articulatory content in the frames. Among tuned implementations of anisotropic diffusion, block-matching filtering, non-local means and pre-smoothed non-local means, every configuration that achieves comparable noise suppression does so at the cost of high-frequency content or of structural fidelity. Under severe added Gaussian, Rayleigh and Rician noise, peak signal-to-noise ratio improves by 7.6 to 11.8 dB and structural similarity roughly triples. An ablation shows that the variance-stabilized pseudo-supervision is an essential element for denoising, and that the effect is attributable to the hard thresholding contained in the stabilization transform.

title: Conformal ordering: Distribution-free predictive inference for orders and rank
summary:
We study distribution-free predictive inference for the ordering and ranking of multiple unobserved outcomes. Although numerous methods, such as conformal prediction, have been developed for prediction and predictive inference of unobserved outcomes, extending them to provide inference for the ordering of multiple outcomes with an interpretable guarantee is not straightforward. To this end, we develop a framework and methodology for uncertainty quantification in predictive ordering.
  Our approach begins by reformulating the problem of determining an ordering among multiple objects as a graph inference problem. Our method adopts a multiple-testing-inspired approach and constructs an uncertainty graph, where each edge represents a confidently inferred pairwise ordering. We develop a distribution-free procedure for constructing a consistent uncertainty graph while controlling either the family-wise error rate or the false discovery rate. Moreover, we show that the resulting graphs naturally yield risk-controlling prediction intervals for the ranks of the outcomes. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed procedure achieves the target guarantees tightly while maintaining reasonable power and prediction-interval widths.

title: Hardness of Coloring $2$-Colorable $3$-Uniform Hypergraphs with $\log^{Ω(1)} n$ Colors
summary: We show that it is quasi-NP-hard to color a $2$-colorable $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices using $O((\log n)^{1/8})$ colors. This exponentially improves the result of Dinur, Regev, and Smyth [Combinatorica'2005], which showed it is quasi-NP-hard to color a $2$-colorable $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices using $O((\log \log n)^{1/3})$ colors.

title: Measuring the Value of Communication in Multi-Agent Tracking Under Finite-Rate Belief Sharing
summary: This paper investigates the value of communica- tion (VoC) in cooperative multi-agent tracking under rate- constrained information exchange. Although prior work has studied distributed tracking, quantized communication, and robust fusion, it remains unclear at what communication rate most of the achievable tracking gain is obtained, beyond which additional communication resources yield only marginal benefit. We consider stationary agents that observe a moving target through heterogeneous range and bearing measurements, perform local extended Kalman filtering (EKF), quantize their posterior state means, and fuse exchanged information via covariance intersection (CI). Performance is evaluated versus communication rate relative to no-communication baselines, a centralized oracle, and a CI-perfect reference. The results show that communication is not uniformly beneficial: very low rates can degrade performance due to coarse quantization, whereas moderate rates recover most of the achievable gain. In the considered scenario, increasing the rate from 4 to 12 bit/s per agent reduces the root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 13.93 m to 6.35 m, while a further increase to 32 bit/s per agent improves it only marginally to 5.93 m. This reveals a clear knee region at moderate rates, beyond which the remaining loss is mainly due to the conservatism of the fusion architecture. Overall, the proposed framework characterizes low-rate degradation, communication-efficient operation, and diminishing returns, while highlighting the joint role of rate and sensing geometry in determining communication benefit.

title: Marginal Composite Likelihood Estimation of Bergomi Models from High-Frequency Option Prices
summary: We develop a theory for estimating the kernel parameters of Bergomi-type stochastic volatility models from option-price time series. The framework allows positive kernels that may be singular at the origin, including the pure power-law kernel of the rough Bergomi model. Using the option-price representation of cumulative forward variance, we formulate the statistical experiment as exact observations of this quantity on increasingly fine time-maturity grids over a fixed horizon. The model has an infinite-dimensional state driven by a single Brownian motion, resulting in a rank-one leading covariance across maturities. Our construction takes maturity differences and then logarithmic time increments. Approximating the resulting diffusion coefficients by maturity-averaged kernels removes the unobserved forward variance curve from the leading term. Positivity of the kernel allows the leading covariance to be recovered from the marginal variances, motivating a weighted marginal composite likelihood contrast. We prove consistency without relative rate restrictions between the time and maturity meshes, allowing the true parameter to lie on the boundary. Under additional regularity and nondegeneracy assumptions and explicit mesh rate conditions, we establish $\mathscr F_1$-stable asymptotic normality, where $\mathscr F_1$ is the terminal model $σ$-field. The Gaussian limit has deterministic sandwich covariance and is independent of $\mathscr F_1$, so the limit is preserved under equivalent changes of probability measure. We also provide sufficient mesh rate conditions for the pure power-law kernel.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Global Climate Policy Cooperation
comment: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning: workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: International climate policy requires coordination among countries whose mitigation decisions impose local costs but generate global benefits. Classical game-theoretic and integrated assessment approaches can study these incentives, but typically rely on prescribed behavioural assumptions or equilibrium concepts. Recent work has therefore explored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning as a way to model climate-policy cooperation as an emergent outcome of repeated strategic interaction. We extend an existing MARL climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism in which agents propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance. This allows us to study how agreement design affects learned mitigation behaviour, compliance, and climate outcomes. In an idealized setting with four homogeneous agents, we find that non-binding agreements do little to overcome free-riding, while moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming. However, excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments, revealing a trade-off between enforcement and participation. We position the framework as a methodological contribution for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations.

title: Readiness-Constrained Pre-Islanding Dispatch for Military Microgrids
comment: 32 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables, submitted to Military Operations Research
summary: Military installation energy readiness depends on having sufficient resources to sustain mission-critical loads throughout a prolonged utility outage. This paper develops a method to help operators manage energy resources during normal grid-connected operation while preserving islanded readiness. A robust viability kernel identifies combinations of battery energy, fuel, and load-shifting capability sufficient to sustain critical load under uncertain demand and photovoltaic generation. A probability bound translates stochastic generator start failures and recovery into a deterministic generator count selected to meet a specified availability requirement at islanding. Case studies for a fourteen-day islanding requirement at 0.999 islanding-entry availability show that advance warning of an outage can be used to prepare resources to meet a higher readiness requirement before islanding begins. The case studies further demonstrate that economic-only operation and the evaluated fixed battery reserve policy can fail to sustain critical load for the required duration, whereas enforcing the resource-dependent requirement preserves readiness at a modest increase in modeled grid-connected operating cost. These results demonstrate how active resource management can preserve long-duration energy readiness. The framework also helps commanders understand how readiness changes with operating conditions, even when the available resources remain the same.

title: Weak Factor Recovery in Sparse Bayesian Factor Models under Exchangeable Shrinkage Process Prior
summary: Sparse Bayesian factor models provide a flexible framework for learning low-dimensional latent structure in multivariate data, but inference on the number of active factors remains challenging when some factors are weak or highly sparse. We study weak factor recovery under a variance based exchangeable shrinkage process (ESP) prior. We derive the posterior factor activation mechanism and show that, conditional on the global and local shrinkage parameters, activation is governed by the standardised loading energy together with the ESP prior activation odds. This yields an explicit activation boundary and clarifies how signal strength, sparsity, the number of observed variables, and the truncation level affect recovery. Simulation experiments show a clear transition between shrinkage and recovery around this boundary and demonstrate that sparsity can substantially affect activation even when raw loading energy is held fixed. They further show that factor activation and recovery of the relative loading pattern across variables can behave differently. These results clarify when weak latent factors become difficult to distinguish from redundant components under ESP shrinkage.

title: ICALL-BENCH: Benchmarking LLM Interprocedural Reasoning in Binary Programs
summary: Recent benchmarks show that LLMs achieve strong performance in both function-level binary understanding and end-to-end binary reverse engineering tasks, but whether LLMs can reason over interprocedural semantics in compiled binaries remains unclear. Function-level benchmarks offer limited visibility into cross-function relationships, while whole-program benchmarks typically evaluate final outcomes of tasks that may be solvable from local clues alone, making it difficult to disentangle interprocedural reasoning from exploration, tool use, execution, and retrieval. To address this limitation, we introduce ICALL-BENCH, a benchmark that directly evaluates whether LLMs and agents can understand and reason over interprocedural semantics in binary programs, using indirect-call target recovery as a measurable probe. ICALL-BENCH covers 50 complete real-world C/C++ programs spanning different complexity levels and multiple optimization configurations, with an average of 74,746 lines of code and 941 functions per program. We further introduce three analysis regimes spanning model-only reasoning, static tool-augmented agents, and Internet-enabled open-world agents to examine how intrinsic reasoning, active information acquisition, and external knowledge each contribute to interprocedural binary analysis. We evaluate five recent LLMs and their corresponding agents. Our results reveal a wide separation across current models and agents, with program-level verifiable success rates ranging from 23% to 81%. They also show that greater information access does not consistently lead to better results, with particularly limited gains on the hardest cases, where deeper interprocedural reasoning remains the primary bottleneck. Uneven performance across models and frequent verifiable failures even under an optimistic evaluation indicate that robust binary interprocedural reasoning remains an open challenge.

title: AFDM-ISAC Design Amalgamating FMCW Radar and Carrier Aggregation
summary: Carrier-aggregation (CA)-assisted affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) is conceived for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW)-inspired dechirping receiver is developed to exploit the inherent pulse-compression property of AFDM chirp subcarriers for accurate delay-Doppler estimation. To further enhance sensing performance, a pair of CA schemes is proposed. The Type-I CA scheme improves sensing accuracy by aggregating echo signals across multiple CA bands prior to radar processing, thereby reducing estimation error with low hardware overhead. The Type-II CA scheme enhances range resolution by effectively enlarging the sensing bandwidth, where chirps from different CA bands are designed to form a continuous set of chirp signals. Based on this principle, variable subcarrier sensing and asynchronous sensing schemes are developed. For the communication receiver, the generalized input-output relationship of AFDM is derived under both fractional delay and fractional Doppler (FDFD) channels. To address the challenge of FDFD estimation, a cross-domain sensing-assisted channel estimation (CDS-CE) scheme is proposed to facilitate time-domain delay-Doppler parameter estimation and affine-domain channel coefficient recovery. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves significant improvements in sensing accuracy and resolution, as well as in channel estimation performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: A case study of hybrid statistical models for analyzing spatio-temporal effects in historical map series of Donau-Ries county
comment: 28 pages, 8 figures. Preprint prepared for Communications in Statistics: Case Studies, Data Analysis and Applications
summary: This case study compares generalized linear models, generalized additive models, and semi-structured deep distributional regression for analyzing settlement patterns in historical land-cover maps. Using four reference years for Donau-Ries county (Landkreis Donau-Ries) in southern Germany, we quantify how distances to agricultural areas, forests, and rivers relate to residential presence, and we evaluate predictive performance through spatial block cross-validation. Classical models yield stable and interpretable distance effects, whereas the semi-structured framework improves prediction once local image context is included. The analysis illustrates a practical trade-off between interpretability, accuracy, and robustness when interpretable covariates are combined with deep components in spatio-temporal data analysis.

title: Set an Exploit to Catch an Exploit: Compiling Public Proofs of Concept into Threat Hunting Rules
summary: Public exploit code for a newly disclosed vulnerability usually appears before any published rule that detects its exploitation. Of the 45 CVEs we evaluate, 37 ever received a Sigma, Elastic or Splunk rule; in 33 the exploit came first, by a median of 22 days. Analysts still write every rule by hand. We present Encore, which compiles a public Python proof-of-concept exploit (PoC) into CVE-specific hunting rules over a web service's existing logs, without running it.
